questions.s: A term baby is born by spontaneous vaginal delivery at a THQ hospital. After being dried and stimulated on a warm surface, he is not breathing and is limp. His heart rate is 80/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give adrenaline through an umbilical venous catheter
Start positive-pressure ventilation with bag and mask
Continue vigorous back rubbing and flicking of the soles
questions.e: An apnoeic baby with a heart rate below 100/min after initial steps needs bag-and-mask ventilation within the first minute of life; effective ventilation is the single most important action in newborn resuscitation. Chest compressions are only started if the heart rate stays below 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

questions.s: A term newborn receives 30 seconds of positive-pressure ventilation with visible chest rise after initial steps. His heart rate is now 50/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilation
Stop ventilation and reassess the heart rate after one minute
Give intravenous normal saline as a volume bolus
questions.e: A heart rate below 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation is the trigger for chest compressions, given in a 3:1 ratio with breaths and with oxygen increased. Volume expansion is reserved for suspected blood loss, and naloxone has no place in the routine resuscitation of an apnoeic newborn.

questions.s: Rukhsana delivers a term baby through thick meconium-stained liquor. The baby is floppy, not breathing and has a heart rate of 70/min after being dried and positioned. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Routine intubation and tracheal suction before any breaths are given
Positive-pressure ventilation with bag and mask
Saline lavage of the airway through an endotracheal tube
Deep oropharyngeal suction for one minute before ventilation
questions.e: Current neonatal resuscitation guidance no longer recommends routine intubation and tracheal suction for non-vigorous babies born through meconium; delaying ventilation worsens hypoxia. The airway is cleared only if obstructed, and bag-and-mask ventilation is started within the first minute.

questions.s: A term baby needs positive-pressure ventilation at birth. Which gas should be used to start ventilation?
o: 100 % oxygen, reduced once the heart rate rises
Air (21 % oxygen), titrated by pulse oximetry
60 % oxygen, fixed until the baby cries
questions.e: Term babies are resuscitated starting with air, with oxygen added according to pre-ductal pulse oximetry targets; starting with 100 % oxygen increases oxidative injury and has been associated with higher mortality. Oxygen is increased to 100 % only if chest compressions are needed.

questions.s: A midwife at a BHU in rural Sindh is trained in Helping Babies Breathe. A newborn is not crying after birth. Within what time after birth should ventilation be started if the baby is still not breathing well after drying and stimulation?
questions.e: The 'Golden Minute' principle teaches that a baby who is not breathing after drying and stimulation should be receiving bag-and-mask ventilation within one minute of birth. Waiting longer while continuing stimulation is the commonest preventable error in newborn resuscitation.

questions.s: During resuscitation of a term newborn, bag-and-mask ventilation is being given but the chest is not rising and the heart rate remains 70/min. What is the most appropriate next action?
o: Give adrenaline through the umbilical vein
Increase the ventilation rate to 100 breaths per minute
Reposition the head, reapply the mask and check the airway
questions.e: Without chest rise, ventilation is ineffective, so corrective steps come first: adjust the mask seal, reposition the head in the neutral position, suction if needed, open the mouth and increase pressure, then consider an alternative airway. Chest compressions are only indicated after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with a heart rate below 60/min.

questions.s: A term baby cries immediately after birth, has good tone and is breathing regularly. The mother is well. What is the most appropriate management of the umbilical cord?
o: Clamp the cord immediately so the baby can be assessed on the warmer
Delay clamping for at least one minute with the baby skin-to-skin
Milk the cord towards the baby five times before immediate clamping
Clamp the cord only after the placenta has been delivered
questions.e: For vigorous term babies, delayed cord clamping for at least 30-60 seconds improves iron stores and haemoglobin in infancy, and can be done while the baby lies skin-to-skin. Immediate clamping is only needed when the baby requires resuscitation that cannot be given with the cord intact.

questions.s: A 3-day-old term baby, Ali, is noticed to be yellow on the face and chest. He is breastfeeding well, active and was not jaundiced on day 1. His serum bilirubin is below the phototherapy line for his age. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Jaundice that appears after 24 hours, peaks around day 3-5 in a well, feeding term baby and stays below treatment thresholds is physiological, caused by a high red-cell turnover and immature hepatic conjugation. Rhesus haemolysis typically causes jaundice within the first 24 hours.

questions.s: A baby girl is noted to be jaundiced 14 hours after birth. Her mother is blood group O Rh positive and the baby is group A Rh positive. Hb is 12.5 g/dL with a raised reticulocyte count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn
Physiological jaundice of the newborn period
questions.e: Jaundice within 24 hours is always pathological, and an O-group mother with an A or B baby points to ABO incompatibility, caused by maternal IgG anti-A or anti-B crossing the placenta. Physiological and breast-milk jaundice never start in the first day of life.

questions.s: A 5-week-old baby boy has been jaundiced since the second week of life. His mother says his stools have become pale and his urine stains the nappy dark yellow. He is gaining weight. Conjugated bilirubin is 3.8 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged conjugated jaundice with pale stools and dark urine in a thriving infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Early diagnosis matters because the Kasai portoenterostomy works best before about 60 days. Breast-milk jaundice is unconjugated and the stools stay yellow.

questions.s: A term baby with significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is started on phototherapy. By which mechanism does phototherapy lower the serum bilirubin?
o: It converts bilirubin into water-soluble isomers excreted without conjugation
It induces hepatic glucuronyl transferase activity
It increases the binding of unconjugated bilirubin to albumin in the plasma
It reduces red-cell haemolysis in the skin capillaries
questions.e: Blue-green light converts bilirubin in the skin into configurational and structural isomers such as lumirubin, which are water soluble and are excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. Enzyme induction is the action of phenobarbital, not light.

questions.s: A 4-day-old term boy of a Pakistani family has severe jaundice (total bilirubin 24 mg/dL) after his mother applied a naphthalene-scented cloth to his cot. Hb has fallen from 17 to 11 g/dL and the direct Coombs test is negative. Mother and baby are each blood group B positive. What is the most likely underlying cause?
o: Hereditary spherocytosis presenting in the newborn period
questions.e: Acute Coombs-negative haemolysis in a boy after exposure to naphthalene (mothballs) is typical of G6PD deficiency, which is common in Pakistan and X-linked. Rhesus disease would be Coombs positive and requires a Rh-negative mother; Crigler-Najjar causes unconjugated jaundice without anaemia.

questions.s: A 5-day-old baby has a total serum bilirubin of 28 mg/dL despite intensive phototherapy. He is now lethargic, feeding poorly and has a high-pitched cry with arching of the back. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue phototherapy and recheck bilirubin in 24 hours
Stop breastfeeding and give formula only
questions.e: Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, hypertonia with retrocollis or opisthotonus, high-pitched cry) are an indication for immediate exchange transfusion regardless of the exact level. Phenobarbital acts too slowly and continuing phototherapy alone risks permanent kernicterus.

questions.s: A 7-day-old term breastfed baby has gradually increasing jaundice. The baby is feeding well, stools are yellow and weight is regained. Total bilirubin is 16 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated; Hb, reticulocytes and blood film are normal. Jaundice is still mildly present at 4 weeks with normal thyroid function. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Breast-milk jaundice causes prolonged unconjugated jaundice in a well, thriving breastfed baby with normal stools and no haemolysis; breastfeeding should continue. Neonatal hepatitis and choledochal cyst cause conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, which is why the conjugated fraction must be measured in prolonged jaundice.

questions.s: A 2-day-old baby born after prolonged rupture of membranes for 30 hours becomes lethargic, feeds poorly and has a temperature of 38.4 °C. Blood culture is taken. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.e: Early-onset neonatal sepsis is mainly due to group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria, so ampicillin plus gentamicin is the standard first-line empirical regimen. Broad combinations including vancomycin are reserved for late-onset hospital sepsis with known resistance patterns.

questions.s: A 10-day-old baby is brought to a BHU with poor feeding. Examination shows redness of the umbilicus extending to the surrounding abdominal skin. Temperature is 38.0 °C and he moves only when stimulated. Under IMCI young infant guidelines, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Clean the umbilicus with gentian violet and review in 2 days
Give oral amoxicillin for seven days at home and review the baby after two days
Give the first dose of intramuscular antibiotics and refer urgently
Apply topical antibiotic ointment and continue breastfeeding
questions.e: Umbilical redness extending to the skin, fever and movement only on stimulation are signs of possible serious bacterial infection, which needs a pre-referral dose of intramuscular antibiotics, prevention of hypoglycaemia and urgent referral. Local treatment is only for local infection with pus or redness confined to the umbilicus.

questions.s: An 8-day-old baby born at home in rural Balochistan stops sucking, then develops stiffness and generalised spasms triggered by touch. He is fully conscious between spasms. The mother received no antenatal care, and the cord was cut with an unsterilised blade. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inability to suck followed by trismus, rigidity and stimulus-triggered spasms in a conscious baby aged 3-14 days, after unhygienic cord care and no maternal tetanus vaccination, is neonatal tetanus. Meningitis usually causes altered consciousness and a bulging fontanelle rather than spasms with a clear sensorium.

questions.s: Which investigation is the gold standard for confirming neonatal sepsis?
questions.e: A positive blood culture confirms bacteraemia and guides antibiotic choice, so it should be taken before the first dose. CRP, white cell counts and procalcitonin are supportive markers that help decide on stopping antibiotics but cannot confirm infection.

questions.s: A 12-day-old preterm baby in a neonatal unit in Karachi develops late-onset sepsis. Blood culture grows Klebsiella pneumoniae that produces extended-spectrum beta-lactamase. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.e: ESBL-producing Gram-negative bacilli hydrolyse penicillins and third-generation cephalosporins, so a carbapenem such as meropenem is the drug of choice. Cefotaxime may appear active in some reports but fails clinically against ESBL organisms.

questions.s: A 6-day-old baby with suspected late-onset sepsis has a bulging anterior fontanelle and a seizure. Blood culture has been taken and he is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Meningitis accompanies a significant proportion of neonatal sepsis and changes the antibiotic choice and duration, so a lumbar puncture should be done in a stable baby with suspected sepsis, especially with seizures or a bulging fontanelle. Imaging may follow but does not diagnose meningitis.

questions.s: In a district of Punjab with high neonatal mortality from omphalitis, the health department wants a single intervention at birth to reduce umbilical cord infection in home deliveries. Which practice is recommended?
o: Applying surma or ghee to the cord stump daily
Covering the cord with a tight sterile bandage for one week
Applying chlorhexidine to the cord stump
Applying gentian violet to the cord after every bath
questions.e: In settings with high neonatal mortality, WHO recommends applying 7.1 % chlorhexidine digluconate to the cord stump in the first week, which reduces omphalitis and deaths. Traditional applications such as ghee raise infection risk, and tight bandaging keeps the stump moist.

questions.s: A baby born at 29 weeks' gestation develops grunting, nasal flaring and subcostal recession within an hour of birth. Chest X-ray shows a diffuse ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms. What is the underlying cause?
o: Congenital pneumonia due to group B streptococcus
questions.e: Respiratory distress syndrome in preterm babies results from surfactant deficiency, causing alveolar collapse that gives the ground-glass lungs and air bronchograms. Retained lung fluid causes transient tachypnoea in term babies, which shows fluid in the fissures rather than ground glass.

questions.s: Saima is admitted at 30 weeks of pregnancy in preterm labour with intact membranes. Which intervention given to her will most reduce the risk of respiratory distress syndrome in the baby?
questions.e: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, reducing respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death. Magnesium sulfate at this gestation is given for fetal neuroprotection, and nifedipine only delays delivery.

questions.s: A 10-day-old baby born at 28 weeks, fed with formula, develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and blood in the stool. Abdominal X-ray shows gas within the bowel wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumatosis intestinalis in a preterm, formula-fed baby with distension and bloody stools is diagnostic of necrotising enterocolitis. Breast milk feeding is protective. Hirschsprung enterocolitis follows delayed passage of meconium and does not typically show intramural gas in a preterm baby.

questions.s: A baby born at 27 weeks' gestation weighing 900 g received prolonged oxygen therapy. At 5 weeks of age the paediatrician arranges a specific screening examination before discharge. Which complication is this screening for?
questions.e: Retinopathy of prematurity is an abnormal retinal vascular proliferation linked to extreme prematurity, low birth weight and oxygen exposure; timely retinal screening allows laser treatment before retinal detachment and blindness. Hearing screening is also done but is not the examination linked to oxygen use.

questions.s: A baby born at 30 weeks has repeated episodes in which breathing stops for more than 20 seconds with bradycardia, without fever or other signs of sepsis. Blood glucose and electrolytes are normal. Which drug is used to treat this condition?
questions.e: Apnoea of prematurity is caused by immaturity of the brainstem respiratory centre, and methylxanthines such as caffeine citrate stimulate breathing and reduce the number of episodes. Sepsis, hypoglycaemia and other secondary causes must first be excluded, as here.

questions.s: A stable low-birth-weight baby of 1.6 kg at a district hospital is ready to leave the incubator. The mother asks how she can keep him warm at home where electricity is unreliable. What is the best advice?
o: Kangaroo mother care with continuous skin-to-skin contact
Several layers of wool blankets in a separate cot
A hot-water bottle placed beside the baby at night
Keeping the room heated with a coal fire at all times
questions.e: Kangaroo mother care keeps a low-birth-weight baby warm through skin-to-skin contact, and also improves breastfeeding and reduces infection and mortality. Hot-water bottles cause burns, and coal fires risk carbon monoxide poisoning.

questions.s: A baby born at 26 weeks becomes acutely unwell on day 3 with a sudden drop in haemoglobin, a bulging fontanelle and hypotension. What is the best initial investigation to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Intraventricular haemorrhage typically occurs in the first days of life in very preterm babies, and bedside cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle confirms it without moving an unstable baby. CT involves radiation and transport, and lumbar puncture does not grade the bleed.

questions.s: At one minute of age a baby has a heart rate of 110/min, a weak irregular cry, some flexion of the limbs, a grimace on suction and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What is the Apgar score?
questions.e: Heart rate above 100 scores 2, weak irregular breathing 1, some flexion 1, grimace 1 and acrocyanosis 1, giving 6. The Apgar score describes the baby's condition but is not used to decide whether resuscitation should start.

questions.s: A term baby born after a prolonged obstructed labour needed 10 minutes of resuscitation. At 3 hours he is lethargic with reduced tone and weak suck, and cord pH was 6.9. Which treatment started within 6 hours of birth improves neurological outcome?
questions.e: For term babies with moderate or severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, cooling to 33-34 °C for 72 hours, started within 6 hours of birth, reduces death and disability. Mannitol and steroids have no proven benefit, and prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended.

questions.s: A term baby with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy develops rhythmic jerking of the right arm and leg on day 1. Blood glucose is 70 mg/dL and calcium is normal. Which drug is first-line?
questions.e: Phenobarbital remains the first-line anticonvulsant for neonatal seizures, after hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia have been excluded or corrected. Valproate is avoided in neonates because of hepatotoxicity, and carbamazepine and ethosuximide are not used for neonatal seizures.

questions.s: A term baby with severe birth asphyxia has passed only 10 mL of urine in 36 hours. Serum sodium is 124 mmol/L, urine osmolality is inappropriately high and there is no oedema or hypotension. What is the most likely cause of the hyponatraemia?
o: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Excess sodium loss through the skin
questions.e: Hypoxic brain injury commonly causes SIADH, giving dilutional hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and low urine output; management is fluid restriction. Diabetes insipidus causes the opposite pattern, with dilute urine and hypernatraemia.

questions.s: A 4.5 kg baby born to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes becomes jittery at 2 hours of age. What is the most likely metabolic cause?
questions.e: Maternal hyperglycaemia causes fetal hyperinsulinism, which persists after birth when the glucose supply stops and produces hypoglycaemia in the first hours. Hypocalcaemia also occurs in infants of diabetic mothers but usually later, around 24-72 hours.

questions.s: A macrosomic baby of a diabetic mother is lethargic at day 2. Hb is 23 g/dL and haematocrit 70 % on a venous sample. What complication does this place him at greatest risk of?
questions.e: Polycythaemia (venous haematocrit above 65 %) in infants of diabetic mothers, caused by fetal hypoxia driving erythropoietin, leads to hyperviscosity with lethargy, hypoglycaemia, jaundice and thromboses such as renal vein thrombosis. Symptomatic babies may need a partial exchange transfusion.

questions.s: A grandmother in Multan wants to give honey and ghutti to her newborn grandson before he is put to the breast. What is the correct advice?
o: Give a small amount of honey only, then start breastfeeding
Give boiled water until the mother's milk comes in
Give no prelacteal feeds and start breastfeeding within one hour
Give formula feeds for the first day so that the mother can rest after delivery
questions.e: Prelacteal feeds such as ghutti, honey or water delay breastfeeding, displace colostrum and introduce infection; honey also carries a risk of infant botulism. Breastfeeding should start within the first hour of birth, and colostrum is all a healthy term baby needs.

questions.s: Why is intramuscular vitamin K given to all newborns at birth?
o: To prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
To prevent rickets in breastfed infants
questions.e: Newborns have low vitamin K stores, poor placental transfer and low amounts in breast milk, so they can develop vitamin K deficiency bleeding; a single intramuscular dose at birth prevents both early and late forms. Rickets prevention requires vitamin D, not vitamin K.

questions.s: A term breastfed baby is weighed on day 5 and has lost 8 % of birth weight. He is feeding 8-10 times a day, passing yellow stools and has 6 wet nappies daily. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Add formula top-ups after every breastfeed until birth weight is regained
Continue exclusive breastfeeding and reweigh in a few days
questions.e: Term babies commonly lose up to about 10 % of birth weight in the first week and regain it by 10-14 days; frequent feeds, yellow stools and good urine output confirm adequate intake. Unnecessary top-ups or glucose water undermine milk supply.

questions.s: A 1.4 kg baby born at 32 weeks is stable in room air but tires and coughs when put to the breast. What is the most appropriate way to feed him?
o: Expressed breast milk by cup or nasogastric tube
questions.e: Coordinated suck-swallow-breathe matures around 32-34 weeks, so a stable preterm baby unable to breastfeed effectively should receive his mother's expressed milk by cup, paladai or nasogastric tube while breastfeeding attempts continue. Bottles interfere with breastfeeding and cow's milk is unsuitable.

questions.s: A newborn has a cleft palate without a cleft lip. The mother wants to breastfeed. Which feeding problem is most expected?
o: Inability to generate suction, leading to poor intake and nasal regurgitation
Choking due to an associated tracheo-oesophageal fistula
questions.e: A cleft palate prevents the baby from sealing the oral cavity and creating negative pressure, causing weak suction, prolonged feeds and milk escaping through the nose. Expressed breast milk by special squeezable bottles or cup and early cleft team review are usually needed.

questions.s: A 3-day-old term baby vomits green fluid after every feed. He passed meconium on day 1 and the abdomen is not distended. He is pink and well perfused. Plain abdominal X-ray shows a 'double bubble' with some gas in the distal bowel. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and an urgent upper GI contrast study shows the position of the duodenojejunal flexure. A double bubble with distal gas fits partial duodenal obstruction including malrotation; rectal biopsy is for Hirschsprung disease.

questions.s: A baby is born at 28 weeks' gestation in a hospital labour room in Lahore. The room is cool. Besides placing the baby under a radiant warmer, which measure best prevents hypothermia in the first minutes?
o: Bathing the baby in warm water immediately
Wrapping the undried body in a food-grade plastic bag or sheet
Rubbing the baby vigorously with a dry towel for two minutes
Applying warm oil massage to the trunk and limbs
questions.e: Very preterm babies lose heat rapidly by evaporation, and placing them undried in a polyethylene bag or wrap under a radiant warmer reduces hypothermia. Vigorous rubbing helps term babies but is less effective for very preterm babies and may injure fragile skin; bathing increases heat loss.

questions.s: During bag-and-mask ventilation of a newborn, which sign is the best indicator that ventilation is effective?
o: Change of the baby's colour from blue to pink
questions.e: A prompt increase in heart rate is the most sensitive sign that the lungs are being ventilated during newborn resuscitation. Colour changes slowly and is unreliable, and crying may take longer to appear.

questions.s: A newborn needs chest compressions. Which technique is recommended?
o: Two thumbs encircling the chest, pressing on the lower third of the sternum
Heel of one hand on the xiphisternum
Two fingers over the upper third of the sternum
Pressing on the left side of the chest over the apex
questions.e: The two-thumb encircling technique on the lower third of the sternum, compressing about one third of the chest depth, produces better perfusion than the two-finger method. Pressing over the xiphisternum risks liver injury.

questions.s: What is the ratio of chest compressions to ventilations during neonatal cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
questions.e: Newborn resuscitation uses 3 compressions to 1 breath, giving about 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute, because neonatal arrest is almost always due to asphyxia and ventilation is the priority. The 30:2 and 15:2 ratios apply to older children and adults.

questions.s: A term newborn's heart rate remains 40/min despite 60 seconds of chest compressions coordinated with effective ventilation using 100 % oxygen. Which route is preferred for giving adrenaline?
questions.e: The umbilical vein gives rapid, reliable central access in the delivery room, and intravenous adrenaline is preferred over the endotracheal route. Intramuscular and subcutaneous routes are too slow in cardiac arrest, and scalp veins are hard to cannulate in a shut-down baby.

questions.s: Nasreen, who is Rh negative, has just delivered a Rh-positive baby. Her indirect Coombs test was negative throughout pregnancy. What should be given to prevent haemolytic disease in her next pregnancy?
o: Intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother during the next pregnancy
Anti-D immunoglobulin to the mother within 72 hours
Rh-negative blood transfusion to the mother
questions.e: Anti-D given to a non-sensitised Rh-negative mother within 72 hours of delivering a Rh-positive baby destroys fetal red cells before she forms her own antibodies. Giving anti-D to the baby would cause haemolysis and offers no protection for future pregnancies.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy had severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion. He now has writhing involuntary movements, deafness and limitation of upward gaze. Which brain region is mainly affected?
questions.e: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) results from unconjugated bilirubin staining the basal ganglia, especially the globus pallidus, plus brainstem nuclei, causing dyskinetic cerebral palsy, sensorineural deafness and upward gaze palsy. Cerebellar damage would cause ataxia rather than athetosis.

questions.s: A term baby is still visibly jaundiced at 3 weeks of age. He is breastfeeding well. What is the most important first investigation?
questions.e: Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby is prolonged and must be assessed with a split bilirubin; a raised conjugated fraction points to cholestasis such as biliary atresia, which needs urgent work-up. Imaging and biopsy follow only if conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is confirmed.

questions.s: A 6-day-old baby born to consanguineous parents has unconjugated bilirubin of 26 mg/dL with no haemolysis, normal thyroid function and normal liver enzymes. Bilirubin does not fall after a trial of phenobarbital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Crigler-Najjar type 1 is an autosomal recessive complete absence of UDP-glucuronyl transferase, causing severe unconjugated jaundice that does not respond to phenobarbital. Type 2 has partial enzyme activity and bilirubin falls with phenobarbital; Dubin-Johnson causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

questions.s: A 4-week-old girl has persistent jaundice, constipation, a hoarse cry, a large tongue and an umbilical hernia. She sleeps most of the day and feeds slowly. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Prolonged unconjugated jaundice with lethargy, macroglossia, constipation and umbilical hernia suggests congenital hypothyroidism, confirmed by high TSH and low free T4. Early levothyroxine prevents intellectual disability.

questions.s: A baby born at 34 weeks is unwell from birth with respiratory distress and a pinkish granular rash. During the last week of pregnancy the mother had a flu-like illness after eating soft unpasteurised cheese. Gram stain of the baby's blood culture shows Gram-positive rods. Which organism is most likely?
questions.e: Listeria is a Gram-positive rod acquired from unpasteurised dairy and causes maternal flu-like illness, preterm labour and granulomatous neonatal sepsis. Ampicillin is included in empirical neonatal regimens partly to cover it; group B streptococcus is a Gram-positive coccus.

questions.s: Under IMCI guidance for the sick young infant up to 2 months old, which respiratory rate is classified as fast breathing?
questions.e: In infants under 2 months a respiratory rate of 60/min or more, confirmed on a repeat count, is fast breathing and is a sign of possible serious bacterial infection. The thresholds of 50 and 40 apply to infants aged 2-12 months and children aged 1-5 years.

questions.s: A 3-week-old baby born at 27 weeks has had a peripherally inserted central catheter for parenteral nutrition for 2 weeks. He develops temperature instability and increased apnoeas. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Coagulase-negative staphylococci colonise skin and form biofilms on plastic catheters, making them the commonest cause of late-onset sepsis in preterm babies with central lines; vancomycin is often needed. Group B streptococcus and Listeria mainly cause early-onset sepsis.

questions.s: A Lady Health Worker wants to prevent neonatal tetanus in her area of rural Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Apart from clean delivery and cord care, which intervention is most effective?
o: Tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine to pregnant women
questions.e: Immunising pregnant women with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine produces antibodies that cross the placenta and protect the newborn; together with clean delivery and cord care, this is the basis of maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination. Routine immunoglobulin or antibiotics for all babies are not used.

questions.s: A 3-day-old baby has a profuse purulent discharge from both eyes with marked swelling of the eyelids. The mother had an untreated vaginal discharge in pregnancy. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum appears in the first 2-5 days with hyperacute purulent discharge and lid swelling, and can perforate the cornea, so it needs systemic ceftriaxone. Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually starts later, at 5-14 days, and is less purulent.

questions.s: A term baby born by elective caesarean section at 38 weeks develops a respiratory rate of 80/min with mild recession at 1 hour. Saturation is 94 % in room air. Chest X-ray shows fluid in the horizontal fissure and prominent perihilar markings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after caesarean section without labour causes transient tachypnoea, with fluid in the fissures, and it settles within 24-72 hours with supportive care. Respiratory distress syndrome mainly affects preterm babies and shows a ground-glass pattern.

questions.s: A 10-day-old baby born at 28 weeks is difficult to wean from the ventilator. He has bounding peripheral pulses, a wide pulse pressure and a continuous murmur below the left clavicle. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis. Which drug is used to close the defect?
questions.e: A haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus in a preterm baby can be closed with a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor such as ibuprofen or indomethacin. Prostaglandin E1 does the opposite and is used to keep the duct open in duct-dependent heart lesions.

questions.s: A baby born at 34 weeks' gestation weighs 1,300 g. How is this baby classified by birth weight?
questions.e: Low birth weight is below 2,500 g, very low birth weight below 1,500 g and extremely low birth weight below 1,000 g, so 1,300 g is very low birth weight. Being 34 weeks, the baby is also small for gestational age, which should prompt a search for the cause of growth restriction.

questions.s: A baby born at 26 weeks was ventilated for RDS and still needs supplemental oxygen at a postmenstrual age of 36 weeks. Chest X-ray shows coarse streaky opacities with areas of hyperinflation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
questions.e: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of prematurity, defined by a continuing oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, after injury from ventilation, oxygen toxicity and inflammation. Persistent pulmonary hypertension presents in the first days of life with severe hypoxaemia in mostly term babies.

questions.s: Why are preterm babies more prone to hypothermia than term babies?
o: They have a lower basal metabolic rate due to thyroid immaturity
They shiver vigorously and exhaust their glycogen stores early
They have a large surface area to weight ratio, thin skin and little brown fat
They sweat excessively in the first week of life
questions.e: Preterm babies lose heat quickly through a relatively large surface area and thin, permeable skin, and have little subcutaneous fat or brown fat for non-shivering thermogenesis. Newborns do not shiver effectively, which is why external warmth is essential.

questions.s: A term baby who needed prolonged resuscitation is examined at 12 hours. He is in coma, completely flaccid, with absent suck and Moro reflexes and needs ventilatory support. How is his hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy best classified?
o: Not graded until an EEG is available
questions.e: Stupor or coma, flaccidity and absent primitive reflexes define severe (stage 3) HIE, which carries a high risk of death or disability. Stage 2 babies are lethargic with hypotonia and often seizures, while stage 1 babies are hyperalert and jittery.

questions.s: A 1-day-old baby born after a difficult delivery has a seizure. Bedside blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. After securing the airway, what is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Oral expressed breast milk by cup
Intravenous phenobarbital loading dose followed by maintenance therapy
Intravenous 10 % dextrose bolus followed by an infusion
questions.e: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia, especially with seizures, needs an immediate intravenous bolus of 10 % dextrose followed by a continuous glucose infusion. Anticonvulsants will not stop a seizure caused by low glucose, and oral feeds are too slow and unsafe in a seizing baby.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy had severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy after birth in a district hospital. Which long-term outcome is most typical of severe HIE?
o: Spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy with intellectual disability
Isolated delayed speech with normal motor skills
questions.e: Severe HIE damages the cortex, basal ganglia and white matter widely, typically producing spastic quadriplegia, intellectual disability, epilepsy and microcephaly. Isolated speech or attention problems are more typical of mild injury or other causes.

questions.s: A term baby is encephalopathic at 6 hours of age. Which finding most strongly supports intrapartum hypoxia-ischaemia as the cause?
o: Umbilical artery pH below 7.0 with a large base deficit
A large cephalhaematoma over the right parietal bone after vacuum delivery
questions.e: Severe metabolic acidosis in umbilical cord arterial blood is objective evidence of significant intrapartum hypoxia-ischaemia. A low 1-minute Apgar is common and non-specific, and meconium or a cephalhaematoma do not indicate brain hypoxia.

questions.s: A baby born to a mother with poorly controlled pre-existing type 1 diabetes has absent sacrum and lower limb weakness. Which congenital anomaly is this?
questions.e: Caudal regression syndrome, with sacral agenesis and lower limb abnormalities, is rare but strongly associated with maternal pre-gestational diabetes. Hyperglycaemia in early pregnancy also increases neural tube and cardiac defects.

questions.s: A mother asks why she should give her baby the thick yellow milk produced in the first days after birth. Which component makes colostrum especially protective?
o: High iron content with very good absorption
questions.e: Colostrum is rich in secretory IgA, lactoferrin and white cells that protect the gut from infection, and it is higher in protein than mature milk. It is the baby's first immunisation, so it should never be discarded.

questions.s: A first-time mother in Hyderabad asks how often she should breastfeed her healthy 4-day-old baby. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Strictly every 4 hours by the clock
Only when the breasts feel full
Every 6 hours with water in between
On demand, at least 8 times in 24 hours
questions.e: Healthy newborns should be breastfed on demand, which usually means 8-12 feeds in 24 hours, including at night; frequent suckling also builds the milk supply. Rigid schedules and water between feeds reduce intake and supply.

questions.s: A 7-day-old breastfed girl has vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice and hepatomegaly. Blood culture grows Escherichia coli and urine is positive for reducing substances but negative for glucose on dipstick. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Galactosaemia presents after milk feeds start with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly and E. coli sepsis; non-glucose reducing substances in urine are a clue. Lactose (breast milk or standard formula) must be stopped and replaced with a lactose-free soy formula.

questions.s: A 6-week-old breastfed baby brings up small amounts of milk effortlessly after most feeds. He is gaining weight well, is content and has no blood in the vomit. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure the parents and continue breastfeeding
Arrange an upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation
questions.e: Effortless regurgitation in a thriving, happy infant is physiological reflux (posseting), which improves as the oesophageal sphincter matures, usually by about 12 months. Investigations and acid suppression are not needed without red flags such as poor weight gain, bilious or bloody vomiting.

questions.s: A 6-day-old exclusively breastfed baby of a first-time mother is brought because he is sleepy. He has lost 15 % of birth weight, has a dry mouth and passes dark urine twice daily. Serum sodium is 158 mmol/L (135-145). What is the most likely cause?
o: Excess sodium in the breast milk caused by a high maternal salt intake
Inadequate milk intake due to ineffective breastfeeding
questions.e: Hypernatraemic dehydration in an exclusively breastfed baby with heavy weight loss and scanty urine is due to insufficient milk transfer, often from poor attachment; it needs slow rehydration and breastfeeding support. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes salt loss with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.

questions.s: Zainab's mother brings her for vaccination. Zainab sits steadily without support, pulls herself to stand, picks up small objects between thumb and finger tips, cries when a stranger approaches and babbles 'mama' and 'dada' without meaning. What is her most likely age?
questions.e: Sitting steadily, pulling to stand, an early pincer grasp, stranger anxiety and non-specific babble fit a typically developing 9-month-old. By 15-18 months a child walks alone and uses several meaningful words.

questions.s: A mother asks by what age her baby should begin to smile in response to her face and voice. What is the expected age for a social smile?
questions.e: A social smile normally appears at about 6 weeks, and absence by 8-10 weeks warrants assessment of vision, hearing and social development. Smiles in the first weeks are usually reflex, not social.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy is not yet walking. He sat at 10 months, says several words and plays well with his siblings. His calves look bulky and he has mild hypotonia. Which initial investigation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Any boy not walking by 18 months should have a creatine kinase measured, because Duchenne muscular dystrophy may present with motor delay before obvious weakness, and calf pseudohypertrophy supports it. Brain imaging is not the first step in isolated motor delay with normal social and language skills.

questions.s: A 9-month-old girl always reaches for toys with her right hand and keeps her left hand fisted. She was born at 30 weeks after a complicated neonatal course. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Brachial plexus injury of the right arm
questions.e: Hand preference before about 12-18 months is abnormal and suggests weakness of the unused hand; with prematurity this points to a left hemiplegic cerebral palsy. A right brachial plexus injury would cause the right arm, not the left, to be unused.

questions.s: A boy at a nursery school in Islamabad rides a tricycle, climbs stairs using alternate feet, copies a circle but cannot yet copy a cross, and speaks in three-word sentences. What is his most likely developmental age?
questions.e: Riding a tricycle, climbing stairs with alternate feet, copying a circle and using short sentences are typical of a 3-year-old. Copying a cross comes at about 4 years and a triangle at about 5 years.

questions.s: A 20-month-old boy says no words. He points to show his mother things, makes good eye contact and enjoys playing peekaboo. He had meningitis at 6 months. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
questions.e: Isolated speech delay with good social interaction suggests hearing loss, and meningitis is an important cause of sensorineural deafness, so a formal hearing test comes first. Every child with speech delay should have hearing assessed before other investigations.

questions.s: While examining a well infant, a doctor holds the baby supine, then lets the head drop back slightly. The baby abducts and extends both arms, then brings them together. By what age does this reflex normally disappear?
questions.e: This is the Moro reflex, which normally disappears by about 4-6 months as cortical control develops. Persistence beyond 6 months, or an asymmetric response, suggests cerebral palsy or a brachial plexus or clavicle injury.

questions.s: Bilal weighed 3.2 kg at birth. Assuming normal growth, approximately what should he weigh at his first birthday?
questions.e: Healthy babies roughly double their birth weight by 4-5 months and triple it by 12 months, so about 9.6 kg is expected. Growth should still be judged by plotting on a WHO growth chart rather than by rules of thumb alone.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy from a poor family in Thar is miserable and apathetic. He has bilateral pitting oedema of the feet and legs, sparse pale hair and areas of peeling, dark skin on the thighs. His weight-for-height is between -2 and -1 SD. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral pitting oedema with flaky-paint dermatosis, hair changes and apathy is kwashiorkor, a form of severe acute malnutrition regardless of weight-for-height. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema but not skin and hair changes or apathy.

questions.s: An LHW screens children aged 6-59 months with a mid-upper arm circumference tape. Below which MUAC is a child classified as having severe acute malnutrition?
questions.e: A MUAC below 115 mm in children aged 6-59 months defines severe acute malnutrition, as do weight-for-height below -3 SD and bilateral pitting oedema. MUAC of 115-124 mm indicates moderate acute malnutrition.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl has a weight-for-height below -3 SD and MUAC of 108 mm. She has no oedema, is alert, has no fever or other medical complications, and eats her RUTF test feed eagerly. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Admission to a stabilisation centre for F-75 feeds
Outpatient therapeutic care with ready-to-use therapeutic food
Advice on family diet and growth monitoring with review in 3 months
questions.e: Children with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition who pass the appetite test can be treated at home in an outpatient therapeutic programme with RUTF, routine antibiotics and weekly review. Admission is for those with complications, poor appetite or severe oedema.

questions.s: A 14-month-old boy with severe acute malnutrition and pneumonia is admitted to a nutrition stabilisation centre. Which feed should be started first?
questions.e: In the stabilisation phase, low-protein, low-sodium F-75 is given in small frequent feeds, because the metabolism of a complicated malnourished child cannot handle a high nutrient load. F-100 or RUTF are introduced in the transition and rehabilitation phases once appetite returns and oedema decreases.

questions.s: A 2-year-old with severe wasting has had watery diarrhoea for 2 days and has sunken eyes and a slow skin pinch. He is alert, with a good pulse and warm hands. Which rehydration fluid is most appropriate?
o: Rehydration solution for malnutrition (ReSoMal) given orally
Intravenous normal saline 20 mL/kg as a bolus
Standard ORS given freely as in Plan B
Intravenous Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg over 6 hours as in Plan C
questions.e: Severely malnourished children have excess body sodium and low potassium and are prone to heart failure, so dehydration without shock is treated orally and slowly with ReSoMal. Intravenous fluids are reserved for shock, and standard ORS given at normal Plan B rates risks sodium overload.

questions.s: Four days after starting nutritional rehabilitation, a severely wasted 3-year-old develops breathlessness, oedema and an irregular pulse. Serum phosphate is very low. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Kwashiorkor developing on top of marasmus
Severe hypocalcaemia from vitamin D deficiency
Congenital heart disease unmasked by recovery
questions.e: Refeeding syndrome follows feeding a starved child too quickly: insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, causing hypophosphataemia with heart failure and arrhythmias. This is why feeds start slowly with F-75 and electrolytes are monitored.

questions.s: A 20-month-old with severe acute malnutrition is anaemic (Hb 8 g/dL) on admission. When should oral iron be started?
o: Immediately on admission with the first feed
Once the child is gaining weight in the rehabilitation phase
Only after a packed red cell transfusion has corrected the anaemia
Iron should not be given during the whole treatment
questions.e: Iron is withheld during stabilisation because free iron promotes bacterial growth and oxidative damage while the child's iron-binding proteins are low; it is started in rehabilitation when the child is gaining weight. Transfusion is reserved for very severe anaemia (below about 4 g/dL) or anaemia with distress.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy who had measles 2 months ago cannot see well at dusk. His conjunctivae are dry and there are foamy triangular grey patches on the temporal side of both eyes. Which deficiency is responsible?
questions.e: Night blindness and Bitot spots are signs of vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia), which measles worsens and which can progress to keratomalacia and blindness. High-dose vitamin A should be given promptly.

questions.s: A 15-month-old girl in Peshawar was exclusively breastfed until 12 months and is kept indoors and fully covered. She has bowed legs, widened wrists and swellings along both sides of the chest. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Congenital hypothyroidism with delayed bone age
questions.e: Prolonged breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, little sun exposure, bowed legs, wide wrists, a rachitic rosary and raised alkaline phosphatase fit nutritional rickets. Scurvy causes painful subperiosteal bleeding and gum disease rather than bowing with metaphyseal widening.

questions.s: A child with suspected rickets has an X-ray of the wrist. Which finding is characteristic?
o: Cupping, fraying and splaying of the metaphyses
Dense sclerotic metaphyseal bands with ground-glass shafts
Periosteal new bone formation along the diaphysis
Multiple wormian bones at the wrist
questions.e: Failure of mineralisation at the growth plate in rickets gives a widened, cupped, frayed and splayed metaphysis, best seen at the wrist or knee. Ground-glass bones with dense metaphyseal lines suggest scurvy.

questions.s: A 4-month-old baby is examined. Pressing on the occipital and parietal bones produces a sensation like pressing a ping-pong ball. The baby is breastfed and the mother has low vitamin D. Which condition does this sign most suggest in this infant?
questions.e: Craniotabes, softening of the skull bones that indent and spring back, is an early sign of rickets in young infants. Craniosynostosis causes a ridged, rigid skull, the opposite of softening.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl has progressive bowing of the legs and short stature despite a good diet and vitamin D supplements. Her mother also has short stature and bowed legs. Serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal, phosphate is low, and urinary phosphate excretion is high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Low phosphate with renal phosphate wasting, normal calcium and vitamin D levels, an affected mother and no response to vitamin D point to X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets, caused by excess FGF23. It is treated with phosphate and calcitriol or with anti-FGF23 therapy, not vitamin D alone.

questions.s: Which set of results is most typical of nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets in a toddler?
o: Calcium high, phosphate high, ALP normal, PTH low
Calcium normal, phosphate low, ALP normal, PTH normal
Calcium low or normal, phosphate low, ALP high, PTH high
Calcium normal, phosphate high, ALP high, PTH low
questions.e: Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium absorption, which triggers secondary hyperparathyroidism; PTH keeps calcium near normal but causes phosphaturia, so phosphate falls and alkaline phosphatase rises with increased osteoblast activity. A normal ALP makes active rickets very unlikely.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy of consanguineous parents has severe rickets with hypocalcaemia that has not responded to adequate vitamin D. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal but 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is very low. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D with very low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D indicates a defect in renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1), an autosomal recessive disorder. Calcitriol bypasses the block; more cholecalciferol cannot be activated.

questions.s: A 5-month-old exclusively breastfed baby, born in winter to a mother who wears full veil, has repeated episodes of carpopedal spasm and then a generalised seizure. Serum calcium is 6.2 mg/dL (8.5-10.5). What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Single large oral dose of vitamin D with oral calcium syrup at home
Slow intravenous 10 % calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring
questions.e: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with seizures from vitamin D deficiency needs slow intravenous calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring, followed by oral calcium and vitamin D. Vitamin D alone acts too slowly to stop seizures, and anticonvulsants do not correct the cause.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease due to posterior urethral valves has knock knees and bone pain. Serum phosphate and PTH are high and calcium is low. What is the main mechanism of his bone disease?
o: Renal phosphate wasting from a proximal tubular defect
Failure of hepatic 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D
questions.e: In chronic kidney disease, reduced nephron mass causes phosphate retention and loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, giving low calcitriol, hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal osteodystrophy). Phosphate is high, unlike tubular phosphate-wasting rickets in which it is low.

questions.s: A baby is born at a THQ hospital in Punjab. According to the Pakistan EPI schedule, which vaccines should be given at birth?
o: BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B birth dose
Hepatitis B, IPV and typhoid conjugate vaccine
questions.e: At birth Pakistan's EPI gives BCG, a zero dose of oral polio vaccine and a hepatitis B birth dose, ideally within 24 hours. Pentavalent, pneumococcal and rotavirus vaccines start at 6 weeks.

questions.s: The pentavalent vaccine given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks in the Pakistan EPI protects against which diseases?
o: Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, polio and measles
Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Diphtheria, tetanus, hepatitis B, rotavirus and pneumococcal (Streptococcus pneumoniae) disease
Pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid
questions.e: Pentavalent vaccine combines DTP with hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b. Polio is covered separately by OPV and IPV, and pneumococcal and rotavirus vaccines are given as separate products at the same visits.

questions.s: A child received the first dose of measles-rubella vaccine at 9 months. At what age is the second dose due in Pakistan's EPI schedule?
questions.e: Pakistan's EPI gives measles-containing vaccine at 9 and 15 months. The second dose protects children who did not respond to the first, which is important because maternal antibody can blunt the response at 9 months.

questions.s: Hira, aged 7 months, is brought to a BHU. Her card shows only the birth doses; she missed all later visits. She is well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Restart the whole schedule from the birth doses
Wait until 9 months and give all missed vaccines with measles-rubella
Give only measles-rubella now as it is the most important vaccine
Give the next due doses today and continue at 4-week intervals
questions.e: Interrupted schedules are never restarted; the child simply continues from where she stopped, giving the next due doses now and the rest at minimum intervals of 4 weeks. Measles-rubella is not given before 9 months in the routine schedule.

questions.s: A 10-week-old boy is brought for his second dose of vaccines. He has a runny nose and a temperature of 37.8 °C, and is feeding well. His mother asks whether the vaccines should be postponed. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Give the vaccines today as scheduled
Give OPV only and postpone the injections
questions.e: A mild illness such as a cold with low-grade fever is not a contraindication to vaccination; postponing leads to missed opportunities. Vaccination is deferred only for a moderate or severe acute illness.

questions.s: At the 14-week EPI visit a child receives the third doses of pentavalent, OPV and pneumococcal vaccine. Which additional vaccine is given at this visit?
questions.e: Inactivated polio vaccine is added at 14 weeks alongside OPV, giving humoral immunity against type 2 poliovirus that is no longer in OPV. Rotavirus vaccine in Pakistan's EPI is a two-dose schedule at 6 and 10 weeks, and BCG is not boosted.

questions.s: A mother brings her 7-week-old baby because a small ulcer with a little discharge has formed on the left upper arm where BCG was given at birth. There are no enlarged lymph nodes and the baby is well. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and keep the site clean and dry
Apply antibiotic ointment and dress tightly
questions.e: A papule that ulcerates and then heals with a small scar over about 2-3 months is the normal response to BCG and needs no treatment. Covering tightly or applying ointments is unnecessary; large suppurative axillary nodes would need assessment.

questions.s: During a supervisory visit to an EPI centre, a vaccinator finds that the refrigerator thermostat failed overnight and some vials froze. Which vaccine is most likely to have been damaged by freezing?
questions.e: Aluminium-adjuvanted vaccines such as pentavalent, hepatitis B, PCV and tetanus-containing vaccines lose potency if frozen, and the shake test detects damage. OPV is stored frozen at central level and is damaged by heat, not freezing.

questions.s: A nurse observes a mother breastfeeding her 3-week-old baby. Which finding indicates good attachment?
o: The baby's chin is away from the breast
More areola is visible below the baby's mouth than above it
The baby's lower lip is turned outward
The baby's cheeks are drawn in with each suck
questions.e: Signs of good attachment are a wide open mouth, lower lip turned outward, chin touching the breast and more areola visible above than below the mouth. Drawn-in cheeks and a chin away from the breast suggest poor attachment.

questions.s: Sadia, 3 weeks after delivery, has a painful, red, hot wedge-shaped area on her right breast and a temperature of 38.5 °C. She is worried about her baby. What is the most appropriate advice regarding breastfeeding?
o: Stop breastfeeding from both breasts until the fever settles
Continue breastfeeding, including from the affected breast
Feed only from the left breast and discard milk from the right
Stop breastfeeding permanently and switch to formula
questions.e: In mastitis, continued effective emptying of the breast is central to treatment, and the milk is safe for the baby; antibiotics such as flucloxacillin are added if symptoms do not settle or the woman is unwell. Stopping feeding causes stasis and increases the risk of an abscess.

questions.s: A mother is diagnosed with sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB when her baby is 1 month old. She starts standard treatment. The baby is well and has no signs of TB. What is the most appropriate plan for the baby?
o: Separate the baby and feed formula until the mother is cured
Start the baby on full four-drug TB treatment
Give BCG only and continue breastfeeding
Continue breastfeeding and give the baby isoniazid preventive therapy
questions.e: After active TB is excluded in the baby, breastfeeding should continue and the infant receives isoniazid preventive therapy; BCG is given after preventive therapy if not already given. TB is not transmitted through breast milk, and separation harms the baby without clear benefit once the mother is on treatment.

questions.s: A breastfeeding mother is prescribed several medicines. Which one is a reason to stop breastfeeding while she takes it?
questions.e: Cytotoxic chemotherapy such as cyclophosphamide passes into milk and can cause neutropenia and other harm in the infant, so breastfeeding is stopped during treatment. Most common drugs, including amoxicillin, paracetamol and metformin, are compatible with breastfeeding.

questions.s: A mother attending a BHU asks when she should start giving her exclusively breastfed baby other foods. What is the correct advice?
o: At 3 months, starting with cereal in milk
At 4 months, if the baby seems hungry
At 12 months, when the baby has teeth
questions.e: WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then nutritious complementary foods from 6 months with continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond. Earlier foods increase diarrhoea risk and reduce breast milk intake, while later introduction leads to growth faltering.

questions.s: A mother says her milk flows well when she relaxes with her baby but stops when she is anxious or in pain. Which hormone mediates the milk ejection (let-down) reflex?
questions.e: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli to eject milk, and it is inhibited by stress, pain and doubt. Prolactin controls milk production rather than its release.

questions.s: Compared with cow's milk, which feature of human breast milk best explains its suitability for young infants?
o: Whey-predominant protein and lower renal solute load
Higher casein content forming a firm curd in the infant stomach
questions.e: Human milk has less total protein and sodium than cow's milk, with whey predominating, so it forms soft, easily digested curds and places a low solute load on immature kidneys. Cow's milk is casein-dominant with high protein and sodium, which is why it is unsuitable before 12 months.

questions.s: A mother of a 2-month-old exclusively breastfed baby thinks she does not have enough milk because the baby feeds often. The baby is gaining weight along the 50th centile and has 6-8 wet nappies a day. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start formula top-ups after each feed
Reassure her that the baby is getting enough milk
Prescribe a drug to increase milk supply
questions.e: Steady weight gain along a centile and 6 or more wet nappies a day are reliable signs of adequate milk intake; frequent feeding is normal. Unnecessary supplements reduce suckling and therefore milk production.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy says no words, does not point to show things, rarely looks at his parents and does not turn when his name is called. He lines up his toy cars for long periods and becomes very upset if they are moved. His hearing test is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Impaired social communication (no pointing, poor eye contact, no response to name) together with restricted, repetitive behaviour and insistence on sameness is characteristic of autism spectrum disorder. In an isolated expressive language disorder the child communicates socially using gestures and eye contact.

questions.s: A 6-month-old baby is seen for routine review. Which fine motor skill is expected at this age?
o: Transferring a toy from one hand to the other
A neat pincer grasp of a small raisin
Building a tower of four cubes
questions.e: At about 6 months infants grasp objects with the whole palm and transfer them between hands. A neat pincer grasp appears at about 10-12 months, and scribbling and building towers of cubes come in the second year.

questions.s: Hamza, aged 14, is the shortest boy in his class and has no signs of puberty. He has always grown at a steady rate just below the 3rd centile. His father also started puberty late but reached normal adult height. Bone age is 11.5 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.e: Steady growth below but parallel to the centiles, delayed puberty, a delayed bone age and a parent who was a late developer are typical of constitutional delay; the child will eventually reach a normal adult height. In familial short stature the bone age matches the chronological age and puberty is on time.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl's height is on the 2nd centile and has followed this centile since infancy. Her father is 160 cm and her mother 148 cm. She is well, examination is normal and her bone age equals her chronological age. What is the most likely cause of her short stature?
questions.e: A healthy child growing steadily along a low centile consistent with short parents, with bone age equal to chronological age, has familial short stature. Turner syndrome should still be considered in short girls, but it usually causes growth falling away from the parental target with dysmorphic features.

questions.s: A mother asks when the soft spot at the top of her baby's head will close. By what age does the anterior fontanelle normally close?
questions.e: The anterior fontanelle usually closes between 12 and 18 months. Delayed closure suggests rickets, hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure or skeletal disorders; the posterior fontanelle closes much earlier, by about 6-8 weeks.

questions.s: Which language skill is typically expected of a 2-year-old child?
o: Combining two words into simple phrases
Telling a story with a beginning and end
Using only one or two words in total
questions.e: At 2 years children typically know about 50 words and join two words together ('more milk'). Full sentences and storytelling develop between 3 and 5 years, while only one or two words at age 2 is delayed and needs a hearing check.

questions.s: A 16-month-old girl with severe acute malnutrition is admitted to a stabilisation centre. She is alert. Her blood glucose is 45 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Wait for the next scheduled F-75 feed in 3 hours and recheck glucose then
Oral or nasogastric 10 % glucose followed by F-75 every 2 hours
questions.e: Hypoglycaemia (below 54 mg/dL) in an alert malnourished child is treated with 10 % glucose or sugar solution by mouth or nasogastric tube, followed by frequent F-75 feeds day and night. Intravenous glucose is used only if the child is unconscious, and 50 % dextrose is too concentrated for children.

questions.s: A 3-year-old with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition is enrolled in an outpatient therapeutic programme. She has no fever or other signs of infection. Which medicine should she receive routinely?
o: Oral iron and folic acid from the first day
Oral furosemide to reduce any fluid overload
questions.e: Children with SAM often have infections without the usual signs, so WHO recommends routine oral amoxicillin even in uncomplicated cases managed as outpatients. Diuretics are never used to treat malnutrition oedema, and injectable antibiotics are for complicated cases.

questions.s: A severely wasted 20-month-old boy is admitted at night. His axillary temperature is 34.6 °C. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Bathe him in warm water to raise the temperature quickly
Leave him uncovered under a fan to prevent fever
Rewarm with skin-to-skin contact or blankets, feed him and treat for infection
Start an intravenous infusion of warmed normal saline and keep the child nil by mouth
questions.e: Hypothermia in SAM is a sign of serious infection and depleted energy; the child should be rewarmed by skin-to-skin contact with the mother or covered warmly including the head, fed promptly and given antibiotics, while hypoglycaemia is checked. Bathing increases heat loss.

questions.s: A nutrition survey in Sindh reports the proportion of children under 5 with stunting. Which measurement defines stunting?
questions.e: Stunting is a low length or height-for-age and reflects chronic undernutrition and repeated infection. Low weight-for-height (wasting) and low MUAC reflect acute malnutrition, while low weight-for-age (underweight) combines both.

questions.s: A 10-month-old girl weaned early onto diluted bottle feeds has severe visible wasting, loose skin folds over the buttocks and an 'old man' face. There is no oedema. She is alert and hungry. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe wasting with loss of muscle and fat, baggy skin and an aged face but no oedema is marasmus, often due to dilute bottle feeds and repeated diarrhoea. Kwashiorkor and marasmic kwashiorkor both require bilateral pitting oedema.

questions.s: An 8-month-old girl, weaned from breast milk at 6 months, has chronic diarrhoea, hair loss and red, scaly, crusted lesions around the mouth, nose and anus and on the hands. She is irritable and failing to thrive. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e: Periorificial and acral dermatitis with alopecia and diarrhoea is the classic triad of acrodermatitis enteropathica, due to an inherited defect of zinc absorption, which often presents after weaning from breast milk. It responds rapidly to zinc supplements.

questions.s: A mother in Quetta wants to prevent rickets in her exclusively breastfed 1-month-old baby. What is the most appropriate preventive measure?
o: A single intramuscular injection of vitamin D every month
questions.e: Breast milk contains little vitamin D, so daily oral vitamin D (usually 400 IU) is recommended for breastfed infants, particularly where maternal deficiency and limited sun exposure are common. Calcium alone does not prevent vitamin D deficiency rickets, and cow's milk is unsuitable before 12 months.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy with epilepsy has been taking phenytoin for 4 years. He now has bone pain and a raised alkaline phosphatase with low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. What is the mechanism of his bone disease?
o: Hepatic enzyme induction increasing vitamin D breakdown
Phenytoin directly inhibits parathyroid hormone release
questions.e: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, phenobarbital and carbamazepine accelerate the hepatic metabolism of vitamin D to inactive products, causing deficiency and rickets or osteomalacia. Children on these drugs need vitamin D supplements and monitoring.

questions.s: In a child with rickets, palpable bead-like swellings are felt along both sides of the anterior chest. Where are they located?
questions.e: The rachitic rosary is the enlargement of the costochondral junctions due to excess unmineralised osteoid at these growth zones. In scurvy, a sharper, angular rosary occurs at the same site but is due to subperiosteal haemorrhage and is often tender.

questions.s: A 2-year-old with nutritional rickets is started on vitamin D and calcium. A wrist X-ray is repeated 3 weeks later. Which finding is the earliest radiological sign of healing?
o: A dense line of provisional calcification at the metaphysis
Complete straightening of the bowed radius
Disappearance of the widened wrist on inspection
questions.e: Within a few weeks of treatment, a dense white line of provisional calcification appears at the metaphysis, separated from the shaft by still-unmineralised osteoid. Bowing corrects much later, over months to years, and growth plates close only at puberty.

questions.s: A child with long-standing rickets has a horizontal groove along the lower chest wall at the level of the diaphragm attachment. What causes this sign?
o: Congenital absence of the lower costal cartilages
Inward pull of the diaphragm on softened ribs
questions.e: Harrison's sulcus forms because the diaphragm pulls inward on poorly mineralised, soft lower ribs during breathing. It can also be seen in chronic respiratory disease with increased work of breathing, such as poorly controlled asthma.

questions.s: Which serum test best reflects a child's body stores of vitamin D?
questions.e: 25-hydroxyvitamin D has a long half-life and reflects intake and skin production, so it is the best measure of vitamin D status. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D may be normal or even high in deficiency because PTH stimulates its production.

questions.s: At the 6-week visit in Pakistan's EPI, a baby receives an injected pentavalent vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine. Which two vaccines are given by mouth at the same visit?
questions.e: At 6 weeks the oral vaccines are OPV-1 and rotavirus vaccine dose 1, given with the injectable pentavalent and pneumococcal vaccines. BCG is given intradermally at birth and typhoid conjugate vaccine is an injection given later in infancy.

questions.s: By which route is BCG vaccine given to a newborn?
o: Intradermal injection in the left upper arm
questions.e: BCG is a live vaccine given intradermally, conventionally over the left deltoid insertion, raising a small bleb. Subcutaneous or deep injection increases the risk of abscess and lymphadenitis.

questions.s: In a district of Punjab, the number of children admitted with pneumococcal pneumonia and meningitis has fallen since a vaccine was added to the EPI schedule at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. Which vaccine is this?
questions.e: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine protects infants against invasive disease and pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae; conjugation to a carrier protein makes polysaccharide antigens immunogenic in infants. The Hib component of pentavalent protects against Haemophilus influenzae type b, not pneumococcus.

questions.s: A 5-month-old boy has been diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency and is awaiting a stem cell transplant. Which vaccine is contraindicated for him?
questions.e: Live vaccines such as OPV, BCG, rotavirus and measles-rubella can cause severe or fatal infection in profoundly immunodeficient children, and OPV can lead to vaccine-associated paralytic polio. Inactivated vaccines are safe, although the response may be poor.

questions.s: A woman who is HBsAg positive gives birth at a district hospital. Besides hepatitis B immunoglobulin, what is the most important step to protect the baby?
o: Delay breastfeeding until the baby is 6 months old
Give the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose within 24 hours
Deliver by caesarean section in future pregnancies
Give the first hepatitis B dose with pentavalent at 6 weeks
questions.e: Hepatitis B vaccine given as early as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours (with immunoglobulin when the mother is HBsAg positive), prevents most perinatal transmission. Breastfeeding is safe and caesarean section is not indicated for hepatitis B alone.

questions.s: Two minutes after receiving her vaccines at an EPI centre, a 4-month-old girl develops widespread urticaria, noisy breathing and becomes floppy and pale. What is the most appropriate first drug?
o: Intravenous hydrocortisone followed by an oral antihistamine
Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
questions.e: Anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory involvement is treated first with intramuscular adrenaline (1:1,000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and must not delay adrenaline.

questions.s: Farzana, 4 months after delivery, exclusively breastfeeds day and night and has not had a period. She asks whether she needs contraception now. Under which conditions is the lactational amenorrhoea method reliable?
o: Baby under 6 months, no periods and fully or nearly fully breastfeeding
Baby under 12 months and breastfeeding at least once a day
Any age of baby, as long as she has no periods
Baby under 6 months, regardless of formula use
questions.e: The lactational amenorrhoea method is over 98 % effective only when all three criteria are met: amenorrhoea, full or nearly full breastfeeding and a baby under 6 months. When any criterion fails, another method should be started.

questions.s: A 6-week-old breastfed baby has frequent, explosive, frothy green stools and seems hungry soon after feeds, although weight gain is adequate. His mother switches breasts every 5 minutes because she worries one side will run dry. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Let the baby finish the first breast before offering the second
Give gripe water after each feed
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give oral rehydration solution instead
questions.e: Switching breasts too early gives the baby mainly lactose-rich foremilk and little fat-rich hindmilk, causing frothy green stools and early hunger. Letting the baby finish one breast first improves fat intake; this is not true lactose intolerance and formula is not needed.

questions.s: A mother on day 4 after delivery has sore, cracked nipples. What is the most common cause?
o: Poor attachment of the baby at the breast
questions.e: Sore and cracked nipples in the first days are usually due to poor attachment, with the baby sucking on the nipple rather than taking a large mouthful of breast. Correcting position and attachment relieves pain; frequent feeding itself does not damage nipples.

questions.s: On day 3 after delivery, Amna's breasts are both swollen, hard and painful, with a tight shiny areola that the baby struggles to grasp. She has no fever and no red patches. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop feeding and bind the breasts tightly
Feed frequently and express a little milk first to soften the areola
Apply ice packs and avoid feeding until the swelling and pain have settled
questions.e: Bilateral engorgement when the milk comes in is relieved by frequent, effective feeding and expressing a little milk to soften the areola so the baby can attach. Binding the breasts or stopping feeds worsens stasis and may lead to mastitis.

questions.s: A health visitor explains the benefits of breastfeeding to a pregnant woman. Which long-term benefit to the mother is well established?
o: Prevention of postpartum depression in every woman
Lower lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer
Permanent weight loss to pre-pregnancy level
questions.e: Breastfeeding reduces the mother's risk of breast and ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes, with greater benefit for a longer total duration. It also helps uterine involution and birth spacing; it does not protect the mother against infections such as hepatitis B.

questions.s: A 2-month-old exclusively breastfed baby is gaining weight well but has had small streaks of fresh blood mixed with mucus in the stools for a week. He is otherwise thriving and examination is normal. His mother drinks a lot of cow's milk. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop breastfeeding and switch to soy formula
Start oral metronidazole for the baby
Arrange an urgent air-contrast enema to exclude intussusception in the baby
Continue breastfeeding while the mother excludes cow's milk from her diet
questions.e: Rectal bleeding with mucus in a thriving breastfed infant suggests cow's milk protein allergic proctocolitis, caused by maternal dietary protein in breast milk. Breastfeeding continues while the mother avoids cow's milk; stopping breastfeeding is unnecessary and soy often cross-reacts.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy in Hyderabad has had watery diarrhoea for 2 days. He is restless and irritable, his eyes are sunken, he drinks eagerly and the skin pinch goes back slowly. He weighs 12 kg. What is the most appropriate management?
o: ORS about 75 mL/kg over 4 hours at the health facility
ORS after each loose stool at home only
Oral metronidazole with a clear-fluid diet and stopping all milk feeds
questions.e: Two or more signs of some dehydration (restless, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, slow skin pinch) call for WHO Plan B: about 75 mL/kg of ORS over 4 hours under observation, plus zinc. Intravenous fluids are for severe dehydration, and antibiotics are not indicated for watery diarrhoea.

questions.s: An 8-month-old girl with 3 days of profuse diarrhoea is lethargic, has very sunken eyes, cannot drink and her skin pinch goes back very slowly. She is not malnourished. Intravenous access is obtained. What is the correct regimen of Ringer's lactate?
o: 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes, then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours
30 mL/kg over 1 hour, then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours
questions.e: In WHO Plan C, infants under 12 months receive 100 mL/kg of Ringer's lactate as 30 mL/kg over 1 hour followed by 70 mL/kg over 5 hours. The faster schedule of 30 minutes then 2.5 hours is for children aged 12 months and older.

questions.s: A 15-month-old child with acute watery diarrhoea and no dehydration is being sent home with ORS. Which other treatment reduces the duration and severity of the episode and the risk of further episodes?
questions.e: WHO recommends zinc for 10-14 days for every child with diarrhoea, as it shortens the episode, reduces stool volume and lowers recurrence over the following months. Antimotility drugs are dangerous in young children and antibiotics are not indicated for watery diarrhoea.
