questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has had diarrhoea with visible blood and mucus for 2 days, with fever and abdominal cramps. He has no signs of dehydration. Which oral antibiotic is recommended by WHO as first line?
questions.e: Bloody diarrhoea in young children is usually due to Shigella, and WHO recommends ciprofloxacin as first-line treatment. Metronidazole is used for amoebiasis only after trophozoites are seen, and nalidixic acid is no longer recommended because of widespread resistance.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl had bloody diarrhoea a week ago. She now looks pale, has passed little urine for 2 days and has petechiae on her legs. Hb is 6.8 g/dL, platelets 42,000/µL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL and the blood film shows fragmented red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury following bloody diarrhoea (often Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or Shigella) define haemolytic uraemic syndrome. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anaemia or renal failure.

questions.s: A 6-month-old formula-fed baby with diarrhoea is irritable, very thirsty and has a doughy feel to the skin. Serum sodium is 162 mmol/L (135-145). What is the main danger of correcting this abnormality too quickly?
questions.e: In hypernatraemic dehydration, brain cells generate osmoles to protect their volume; if sodium falls quickly, water moves into the cells, causing cerebral oedema and seizures, so correction is slow over about 48 hours. Central pontine myelinolysis is the risk of correcting hyponatraemia too quickly.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy has had loose watery stools for 17 days. He has no blood in the stool and no dehydration, but has lost some weight. How should this episode be classified under IMCI?
o: Chronic diarrhoea due to coeliac disease
questions.e: Diarrhoea lasting 14 days or more is persistent diarrhoea; without dehydration it is managed at home with continued feeding, possibly reduced lactose, zinc and multivitamins, with follow-up in 5 days. Dysentery is defined by blood in the stool, not duration.

questions.s: A 14-month-old child admitted with severe watery diarrhoea is rehydrated intravenously. On day 2 he is hypotonic, his abdomen is distended with absent bowel sounds and the ECG shows flattened T waves with U waves. Which abnormality is most likely?
questions.e: Large potassium losses in diarrhoeal stool cause hypokalaemia, which produces muscle weakness, paralytic ileus and ECG changes of flat T waves and U waves. ORS and Ringer's lactate both contain potassium, which helps prevent this.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl in a village near Larkana has had cough for 3 days. Her respiratory rate is 46/min on two counts. There is no chest indrawing, stridor or danger sign. How should she be managed under IMCI?
o: Refer urgently after a first dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone
Give a cough syrup and review in 7 days
Give oral amoxicillin and review in 3 days
questions.e: For a child aged 12 months to 5 years, a respiratory rate of 40/min or more is fast breathing, and without danger signs this is pneumonia treated at home with oral amoxicillin and follow-up in 3 days. Referral is for severe pneumonia, such as a child with a danger sign.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy had measles 2 weeks ago. He is now very ill with high fever and breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation with several thin-walled air-filled cysts. Which organism is most likely?
questions.e: Pneumatoceles complicating a severe pneumonia, especially after measles, suggest Staphylococcus aureus, which can also cause empyema and pneumothorax. Treatment includes an anti-staphylococcal drug such as cloxacillin. Pneumococcal pneumonia usually causes lobar consolidation without cysts.

questions.s: A 4-month-old boy has had a runny nose for 2 days followed by cough, fast breathing and difficulty feeding. There are fine crackles and wheeze throughout the chest. SpO2 is 89 % in air. It is winter. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Nebulised salbutamol every 4 hours until the wheeze settles
Oxygen, nasal suction and support for feeding
questions.e: This is bronchiolitis, usually due to RSV, and treatment is supportive: oxygen for hypoxaemia, gentle nasal suction and feeding support by nasogastric tube if needed. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics do not improve outcomes in typical bronchiolitis.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl wakes at night with a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor at rest after a 2-day cold. She is not drooling and is drinking. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis) causes barking cough and stridor, and a single dose of oral dexamethasone reduces airway swelling; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe distress. Salbutamol acts on the lower airways and does not help upper airway oedema.

questions.s: A 4-year-old unvaccinated boy has a 6-hour history of high fever. He sits leaning forward, drooling, with soft stridor and looks toxic. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Send him to the radiology department for an urgent lateral X-ray of the neck
Keep him calm and arrange airway control by a senior anaesthetist
Insert an intravenous line and take blood cultures
questions.e: Acute epiglottitis, usually due to Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children, can cause sudden complete airway obstruction if the child is upset. Throat examination, cannulation or sending him to radiology may precipitate obstruction; the airway is secured by experienced staff first.

questions.s: A 5-month-old girl who has missed her vaccines has had bouts of coughing for 2 weeks, followed by a gasp and vomiting. Between bouts she looks well. White cell count is 32,000/µL with 78 % lymphocytes. What is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop or post-tussive vomiting and marked lymphocytosis in an unvaccinated infant suggests pertussis, which is treated with a macrolide such as azithromycin; contacts may need prophylaxis. Doxycycline is avoided in young children.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy treated for right lower lobe pneumonia for 6 days still has fever. The right lower chest is stony dull with absent breath sounds. Ultrasound shows a loculated collection, and aspirated fluid is turbid with pH 6.9. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Change to oral antibiotics and discharge
Intercostal chest drain with continued intravenous antibiotics
Repeat chest X-ray in one week
questions.e: Turbid fluid with a low pH indicates empyema, which needs drainage with a chest drain (often with fibrinolytics) in addition to intravenous antibiotics; surgery is considered if drainage fails. Continuing antibiotics alone leaves an infected collection undrained.

questions.s: A 20-month-old boy started coughing suddenly while eating peanuts with his siblings. Two days later he has a persistent cough and wheeze over the right side only. An expiratory chest X-ray shows a hyperinflated right lung. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Sudden choking followed by unilateral wheeze and air trapping on expiratory film indicates an inhaled foreign body acting as a ball valve, which must be removed by rigid bronchoscopy. Bronchodilators and physiotherapy delay definitive treatment.

questions.s: Under IMCI, which finding in a sick child aged 2 months to 5 years is a general danger sign?
questions.e: The general danger signs are inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, and lethargy or unconsciousness; any one of them requires urgent attention and usually referral. Fever, ear discharge and pallor are assessed and classified separately.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl brought to a BHU with cough and fever is lethargic and hard to wake. Her respiratory rate is 48/min. What is the most appropriate action under IMCI?
o: Give oral amoxicillin and review in 2 days
Give the first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and refer urgently
Give paracetamol and oral fluids and observe in the BHU for the next 4 hours
Give salbutamol and reassess in 30 minutes
questions.e: A general danger sign such as lethargy in a child with cough classifies as severe pneumonia or very severe disease, which needs a pre-referral dose of antibiotic and urgent referral to hospital. Home treatment with oral amoxicillin is only for pneumonia without danger signs.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has had pus draining from his left ear for 3 weeks. He has no fever and no swelling behind the ear. How should this be managed under IMCI?
o: Dry the ear by wicking and give topical quinolone ear drops
questions.e: Ear discharge for 14 days or more without tender swelling behind the ear is a chronic ear infection, managed by drying the ear with wicks and topical quinolone drops, with follow-up in 5 days. Oral amoxicillin is for acute ear infection (pus for less than 14 days), and oils or other substances should not be put in the ear.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl attending a BHU has some palmar pallor but not severe pallor. She is not malnourished and has had no deworming in the past year. What is the most appropriate management under IMCI?
o: Give iron, a dose of albendazole, and review in 14 days
Give a single dose of vitamin A and review growth in 6 months
questions.e: Some palmar pallor is classified as anaemia and treated with oral iron and an anthelminthic such as albendazole (for children aged 1 year or more without a dose in the last 6 months), with follow-up in 14 days and malaria testing in malaria areas. Severe palmar pallor needs urgent referral.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy in a malaria-endemic area of Sindh has had fever for 2 days. He has no general danger signs and no stiff neck. According to IMCI, what should be done next?
o: Do a malaria rapid diagnostic test
Give oral amoxicillin for presumed bacterial infection
questions.e: IMCI requires a malaria test (RDT or microscopy) for every febrile child in a malaria-risk area, and antimalarials are given only if it is positive. Antibiotics are not given for fever alone without a bacterial cause identified.

questions.s: A 15-month-old boy is classified as having pneumonia (fast breathing, no danger signs) at a BHU and started on oral amoxicillin. When should he be brought back for follow-up if he does not get worse?
questions.e: IMCI advises a follow-up visit after 3 days for pneumonia; if breathing is slower and fever lower he completes the course, but if he is worse or has developed a danger sign he is referred. Mothers are also told to return immediately if the child cannot drink or becomes sicker.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl in a high malaria-risk district has fever and a stiff neck. She is drowsy. The BHU cannot do a lumbar puncture. What is the most appropriate pre-referral treatment?
o: Oral artemether-lumefantrine with oral paracetamol, then refer the same day
Parenteral antibiotic plus rectal or IM artesunate, then refer
Oral amoxicillin and review the next day
questions.e: Fever with a stiff neck is very severe febrile disease, and in a high malaria-risk area the child may have meningitis or severe malaria, so a first dose of an appropriate parenteral antibiotic and pre-referral artesunate are each given, hypoglycaemia is prevented, and she is referred urgently. Oral drugs are inappropriate in a drowsy child.

questions.s: A 6-week-old baby is seen for a vaccination visit. He is feeding well and gaining weight. There is a harsh grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. He is pink. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Atrial septal defect of secundum type
questions.e: A harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge in an acyanotic infant suggests a VSD, the commonest congenital heart defect; small defects often close spontaneously. An ASD gives a soft ejection murmur in the pulmonary area with fixed splitting of S2.

questions.s: A 1-year-old boy has been mildly cyanosed since 3 months of age. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge and a single second heart sound. Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with reduced lung markings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tetralogy of Fallot (VSD, right ventricular outflow obstruction, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy) causes cyanosis after the neonatal period, an ejection murmur from the outflow tract and a boot-shaped heart with oligaemic lungs. Transposition presents with marked cyanosis in the first days of life.

questions.s: An 18-month-old girl with known tetralogy of Fallot becomes deeply cyanosed, irritable and breathless after crying. Her murmur has become much softer. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Place her in the knee-chest position and give oxygen
Start a prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the ductus
questions.e: In a hypercyanotic (tet) spell, infundibular spasm reduces pulmonary flow and the murmur softens; knee-chest positioning raises systemic vascular resistance and pushes blood into the lungs, along with oxygen and then morphine, fluids or propranolol. Digoxin and diuretics worsen the spell.

questions.s: A term baby becomes markedly cyanosed on day 1 of life with SpO2 of 65 % that does not improve with oxygen. There is no significant murmur and no respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows a narrow mediastinum with an 'egg-on-a-string' heart. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: High-flow oxygen by head box and close observation
questions.e: Transposition of the great arteries depends on mixing through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, so prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open until balloon atrial septostomy and the arterial switch operation. Indomethacin would close the duct and could be fatal.

questions.s: A 1-year-old girl with bilateral cataracts and sensorineural deafness has a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle and bounding pulses. Her mother had a fever and rash in early pregnancy. What is the most likely cardiac lesion?
questions.e: Congenital rubella syndrome classically combines cataracts, deafness and heart disease, most often a patent ductus arteriosus or peripheral pulmonary stenosis. A continuous machinery murmur with bounding pulses is typical of PDA.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy has headaches and a blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg in the right arm. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial pulse. There is a systolic murmur over the back. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Renal artery stenosis from fibromuscular dysplasia
questions.e: Upper limb hypertension with radio-femoral delay and weak femoral pulses, plus a murmur heard posteriorly, indicates coarctation of the aorta; rib notching may be seen on X-ray in older children. Renal and endocrine causes do not cause radio-femoral delay.

questions.s: An 8-year-old girl has a soft ejection systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space. The second heart sound is widely split and the split does not vary with respiration. ECG shows right bundle branch block. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of a secundum atrial septal defect, where increased right heart flow causes a pulmonary flow murmur and often a partial RBBB pattern. An innocent murmur has normal physiological splitting that varies with breathing.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy had a loud murmur from a large VSD diagnosed in infancy, but the family declined surgery. He is now cyanosed with clubbing, the murmur has become soft, and the pulmonary component of S2 is very loud. What has most likely happened?
o: Development of infective endocarditis involving the right heart valves
Reversal of the shunt due to pulmonary vascular disease
questions.e: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when long-standing left-to-right shunting causes irreversible pulmonary hypertension, so the shunt reverses, causing cyanosis, clubbing, a loud P2 and a quieter murmur. At this stage closing the defect is contraindicated.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has puffiness around the eyes for a week and now swollen legs and scrotum. Blood pressure is normal. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and cholesterol is raised. Complement C3 is normal. What is the most likely histological finding on biopsy if done?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome in a young child with normal blood pressure, no haematuria and normal complement is most often minimal change disease, which is steroid sensitive; biopsy is usually not needed. Membranous nephropathy is more typical of adults or hepatitis B-associated disease.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl presents with her first episode of typical nephrotic syndrome. She is normotensive and has no haematuria. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.e: Most children with typical nephrotic syndrome have minimal change disease and respond to oral corticosteroids, which are started without a biopsy. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease, and albumin is only for symptomatic hypovolaemia or severe oedema.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome in relapse develops fever, diffuse abdominal pain and tenderness with guarding. He has gross ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Children with nephrotic syndrome lose immunoglobulins and complement factors in the urine and have ascites, making them prone to spontaneous peritonitis, most often due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Prompt parenteral antibiotics are needed after ascitic tap and cultures.

questions.s: A 13-year-old girl presents with oedema and heavy proteinuria. Which additional finding would most strongly indicate a renal biopsy before starting treatment?
questions.e: Age over about 12 years, persistent hypertension, macroscopic haematuria, impaired renal function or low complement suggest a cause other than minimal change disease, so a biopsy is done before treatment. High cholesterol and low albumin are expected features of any nephrotic syndrome.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden flank pain, macroscopic haematuria and an enlarged left kidney on ultrasound. Which mechanism best explains this complication?
o: Urinary loss of antithrombin III and increased hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Immune complex deposition in the renal veins
Hypertensive damage to the renal artery
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable because small anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III are lost in the urine while the liver increases fibrinogen and other clotting factors, compounded by haemoconcentration; renal vein thrombosis is one result. Steroids do not cause thrombocytopenia.

questions.s: The mother of a 5-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is taught to test his first morning urine at home with a dipstick. Which result defines a relapse?
o: Trace protein on a single day
questions.e: A relapse is defined as urine protein of 3+ (or more) on dipstick for 3 consecutive days, and early recognition allows prompt treatment before significant oedema. Remission is defined as trace or negative protein for 3 consecutive days.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl in Faisalabad has cola-coloured urine, puffy eyes and a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg. She had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. Urine shows red cell casts and 1+ protein. Serum C3 is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension and oedema 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection, with low C3, indicates post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which usually resolves with supportive care. IgA nephropathy causes haematuria within a day or two of an infection and complement is normal.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy with a temperature of 39.5 °C from a viral illness has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes. One hour later he is alert, playful and has no neck stiffness or focal signs. This is his first seizure. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start regular oral sodium valproate until 5 years of age
Treat the fever, explain and reassure the parents
Perform a CT scan of the brain
questions.e: A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes, does not recur within 24 hours and occurs between 6 months and 5 years; with full recovery and no signs of meningitis, management is treating the fever source and educating the parents. EEG, imaging and anticonvulsants are not indicated.

questions.s: The parents of a 2-year-old girl who had a simple febrile seizure ask how they can prevent another one. What is the most accurate advice?
o: Give paracetamol regularly during every fever to prevent seizures
Give a daily anticonvulsant until she is 5 years old
Febrile seizures may recur, and antipyretics do not prevent them
Sponge her with cold water at the first sign of fever
questions.e: About a third of children have a further febrile seizure, but antipyretics do not reduce the risk, and long-term anticonvulsants are not recommended because their side effects outweigh benefit. Parents should be taught first aid and when to seek help for a prolonged seizure.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy with known epilepsy has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home for 6 minutes. The ambulance crew has no intravenous access. Which is the most appropriate first drug?
questions.e: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more needs a benzodiazepine; without intravenous access, buccal (or intranasal) midazolam or rectal diazepam is given. Phenytoin must not be given intramuscularly and phenobarbital needs intravenous access; both are second-line drugs.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl's teacher reports that she stares blankly many times a day for a few seconds, with eyelid flickering, then carries on as if nothing happened. An episode is provoked in clinic by asking her to hyperventilate. Which EEG finding is expected?
questions.e: Childhood absence epilepsy causes brief, frequent staring episodes provoked by hyperventilation, with generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG; ethosuximide or valproate are used. Centrotemporal spikes are seen in self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, which causes nocturnal focal seizures.

questions.s: A 6-month-old boy has clusters of sudden flexion of the trunk and arms with head nodding, mostly on waking. He has stopped smiling and lost head control. Examination with a Wood's lamp shows several pale oval patches on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Clusters of flexor spasms with developmental regression in infancy are infantile spasms, and hypopigmented ash-leaf macules point to tuberous sclerosis, a common cause; the EEG typically shows hypsarrhythmia and vigabatrin is the preferred drug in tuberous sclerosis. Benign sleep myoclonus occurs only in sleep with normal development.

questions.s: An 18-month-old girl cries vigorously when her toy is taken, holds her breath in expiration, turns blue, goes limp and briefly jerks, then recovers fully within a minute. This has happened several times, always after upset. Hb is 9.4 g/dL with microcytosis. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Arrange an urgent EEG and MRI brain
Reassure the parents and treat the iron deficiency
questions.e: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are triggered by crying or upset, may end with brief jerks, and are benign; they become less frequent with age. Iron deficiency is associated and treating it reduces the spells. Anticonvulsants and neuroimaging are not needed.

questions.s: An 8-month-old girl has a 2-minute generalised seizure with a temperature of 39 °C. One hour later she remains irritable and drowsy, and the anterior fontanelle is bulging. She has had no antibiotics. What is the most appropriate investigation after stabilisation?
questions.e: In an infant with fever and seizure, persisting drowsiness, irritability and a bulging fontanelle suggest bacterial meningitis, so CSF examination is essential (provided there are no contraindications such as signs of raised pressure with focal deficits or shock). Antibiotics should not be delayed if the lumbar puncture cannot be done promptly.

questions.s: A healthy 8-year-old boy has had three episodes in which he woke at night with twitching of the right side of his face, drooling and inability to speak, while fully aware. Development and examination are normal. EEG shows centrotemporal spikes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief nocturnal focal seizures involving the face and throat with preserved awareness, in an otherwise normal school-age child with centrotemporal spikes, are typical of self-limited (benign rolandic) epilepsy, which remits by adolescence. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome causes multiple seizure types with intellectual disability.

questions.s: A 3-year-old unvaccinated girl in Karachi has had fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes for 3 days. On the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars there are tiny white spots on a red base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa are diagnostic of measles in the prodrome, before the rash appears. Rubella is milder with lymphadenopathy, and scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy is admitted with measles. Which supplement given to all children with measles reduces complications and mortality?
questions.e: WHO recommends vitamin A for every child with measles, on two consecutive days, because it reduces severe complications, blindness and death. Zinc is recommended for diarrhoea, not specifically for measles.

questions.s: During a measles outbreak in a camp for displaced families, several young children die. Which complication is the most common cause of death from measles in children?
questions.e: Pneumonia, either viral or secondary bacterial, causes most measles deaths in children, with diarrhoea and malnutrition contributing. Encephalitis is serious but much less frequent, and SSPE appears years later.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy who had measles at 1 year of age has had 6 months of declining school performance and personality change, followed by repetitive jerks of the limbs. EEG shows periodic high-voltage complexes. Which finding would confirm the diagnosis?
o: Raised measles antibody titres in the CSF
Oligoclonal bands specific for multiple sclerosis
questions.e: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a fatal late complication of measles infection in early childhood, presenting years later with cognitive decline, myoclonus and periodic EEG complexes; high measles antibody levels in CSF confirm it. Measles IgM indicates acute infection, not SSPE.

questions.s: An 11-month-old girl who has never been vaccinated was in the same room as her cousin with measles yesterday. She is well. What is the most appropriate step to prevent measles in her?
o: Wait and give vitamin A if a rash appears
questions.e: A measles-containing vaccine given within 72 hours of exposure can prevent or modify disease in children aged 6 months or more; immunoglobulin within 6 days is an alternative for those who cannot be vaccinated. Antivirals and antibiotics do not prevent measles.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl developed a measles rash yesterday. Her mother asks when she can go back to school without infecting others. What is the correct advice?
o: 4 days after the onset of the rash
When the rash has completely faded
questions.e: Measles is infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears, so children are excluded until 4 days after rash onset. The rash may leave brownish staining for longer, which is not a sign of infectivity.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl has a mild fever and a pink maculopapular rash that started on the face and spread over the body within a day. She is not unwell. There are tender enlarged postauricular and suboccipital lymph nodes. She has no cough or conjunctivitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mild illness with a rapidly spreading rash and prominent postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy is typical of rubella. Measles causes a much sicker child with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis before the rash.

questions.s: A 9-month-old boy of first-cousin parents has increasing pallor and a swollen abdomen. He has hepatosplenomegaly. Hb is 5.6 g/dL, MCV 58 fL, and the film shows target cells and nucleated red cells. Which investigation will confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe microcytic anaemia with hepatosplenomegaly appearing after 6 months, when HbF production falls, suggests beta-thalassaemia major; haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC shows mainly HbF with little or no HbA. Osmotic fragility testing is for hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.s: Before marriage, Usman has a blood count showing Hb 12.9 g/dL, MCV 63 fL, MCH 20 pg and red cell count 6.4 x 10^12/L. Serum ferritin is normal. HbA2 is 5.1 %. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Marked microcytosis with a high red cell count, normal ferritin and raised HbA2 above 3.5 % is beta-thalassaemia trait. If his partner is also a carrier, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of thalassaemia major, so partner screening and counselling are important.

questions.s: A 10-year-old girl with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia is started on an oral iron chelator. Her weekly blood counts are monitored because the drug can cause agranulocytosis. Which chelator is she taking?
questions.e: Deferiprone can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis, so weekly neutrophil counts are required. Deferasirox, another oral chelator, mainly causes renal and hepatic toxicity, while desferrioxamine is given by subcutaneous infusion.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy with beta-thalassaemia major has received regular transfusions with poor adherence to chelation. Which is the most common cause of death in such patients?
o: Cardiac failure and arrhythmias from myocardial iron
questions.e: Myocardial iron deposition causing heart failure and arrhythmias is the leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, especially with poor chelation; cardiac T2* MRI assesses cardiac iron. Infection and liver disease are important but less common causes of death.

questions.s: A 4-year-old with beta-thalassaemia major attends a thalassaemia centre in Lahore for monthly transfusions. To which pre-transfusion haemoglobin level should transfusions be aimed?
questions.e: Keeping the pre-transfusion haemoglobin at about 9-10.5 g/dL suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, preventing bone deformity, splenomegaly and growth failure while limiting iron loading. Lower levels allow marrow expansion, and higher levels add iron without extra benefit.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy with thalassaemia has massive splenomegaly with increasing transfusion needs, and splenectomy is planned. Which measure is most important to prevent the main long-term risk of the operation?
o: Vaccination against pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus with daily oral penicillin
questions.e: After splenectomy the main risk is overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria, so vaccines against pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus are given at least 2 weeks before surgery, followed by penicillin prophylaxis and urgent assessment of any fever. Chelation must continue.

questions.s: Saima and her husband are both beta-thalassaemia carriers. Their first child has thalassaemia major. She is now 8 weeks pregnant and wants to know whether the fetus is affected as early as possible. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.e: Chorionic villus sampling at 11-13 weeks allows DNA analysis for the parental mutations and gives the earliest reliable result, so a decision can be made in the first trimester. Amniocentesis is later and fetal blood sampling is rarely needed now.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl has had loose stools for a day. She is alert, drinking normally and has no sunken eyes; the skin pinch goes back immediately. Her mother is told to give extra fluid at home. How much ORS should she give after each loose stool?
o: Only as much as the child asks for, no fixed amount
questions.e: In WHO Plan A, children aged 2-10 years receive 100-200 mL of ORS after each loose stool, and children under 2 years 50-100 mL, together with zinc and continued feeding. Waiting for the child to ask risks dehydration developing at home.

questions.s: WHO and UNICEF replaced the original ORS with a reduced-osmolarity formula. What is the main clinical advantage of the low-osmolarity ORS?
o: It provides enough calories to replace feeding
It reduces stool output and vomiting and the need for intravenous fluids
It eliminates the need for zinc supplementation
It corrects hypernatraemia more rapidly than the original ORS
questions.e: Low-osmolarity ORS (with less sodium and glucose) reduces stool volume, vomiting and unscheduled intravenous therapy compared with the older formula, while remaining safe in cholera. Feeding and zinc are still needed alongside it.

questions.s: A pharmacist in Rawalpindi suggests loperamide syrup for a 2-year-old with acute watery diarrhoea. Why should antimotility drugs be avoided in young children with diarrhoea?
o: They interfere with the absorption of ORS
They cause rebound diarrhoea after stopping
They may cause ileus, drowsiness and serious toxicity without reducing fluid loss
They are only effective in bloody diarrhoea
questions.e: Antimotility drugs can cause paralytic ileus, respiratory depression and death in young children, and they hide fluid that continues to pool in the gut rather than reducing losses. Treatment is ORS, zinc and continued feeding.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy from a village using an untreated water supply has had 3 weeks of foul-smelling, greasy, bulky stools, abdominal bloating and weight loss. There is no blood in the stool. Stool microscopy shows pear-shaped flagellated trophozoites. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Giardia lamblia causes malabsorption with greasy, foul stools and bloating, and its trophozoites are pear-shaped with flagella; metronidazole or tinidazole is effective. Albendazole is used for intestinal worms and praziquantel for tapeworm and schistosomiasis.

questions.s: An 8-month-old infant is admitted in winter with vomiting followed by profuse watery diarrhoea and fever. Several infants in the ward have the same illness. Which organism is the most common cause of severe watery diarrhoea in infants worldwide?
questions.e: Rotavirus is the commonest cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants and young children, typically with vomiting and fever, and is preventable with the oral rotavirus vaccine given in Pakistan's EPI. Shigella and Entamoeba cause bloody diarrhoea.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has fever, cough and right lower lobe consolidation on chest X-ray. Which organism is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia in children of this age?
questions.e: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial cause of pneumonia in young children, and amoxicillin is the first-line oral treatment. Mycoplasma is more common in school-age children, and Staphylococcus aureus causes severe pneumonia with complications such as pneumatoceles.

questions.s: An 18-month-old girl admitted with severe pneumonia has an SpO2 of 86 % in room air. Below which SpO2 does WHO recommend giving oxygen to children at low altitude?
questions.e: WHO recommends oxygen for children with SpO2 below 90 % at sea level, which identifies hypoxaemia, a major risk factor for death in childhood pneumonia. Pulse oximetry should be used for every child admitted with pneumonia.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl has had a dry cough, headache, low-grade fever and malaise for 10 days. Chest examination shows a few crackles, but the chest X-ray shows more extensive patchy infiltrates than expected. Several classmates are ill. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.e: Atypical pneumonia in a school-age child, with gradual onset, headache, dry cough and an X-ray worse than the examination, suggests Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which lacks a cell wall and therefore needs a macrolide. Beta-lactams such as amoxicillin are ineffective against it.

questions.s: A 14-month-old boy is admitted to a district hospital with cough, fever, lethargy and inability to drink. He has chest indrawing and SpO2 of 88 %. Which antibiotic regimen does WHO recommend as first line?
questions.e: For severe pneumonia in children aged 2-59 months, WHO recommends parenteral ampicillin or benzylpenicillin with gentamicin, with ceftriaxone as second line if this fails. Oral amoxicillin is for pneumonia without danger signs.

questions.s: A 5-month-old baby has bronchiolitis during a winter outbreak. Which virus is the most common cause?
questions.e: Respiratory syncytial virus causes most bronchiolitis in infants, peaking in winter, with coryza followed by cough, wheeze, crackles and feeding difficulty. Other viruses cause a minority of cases.

questions.s: A medical officer at a rural health centre in Pakistan uses the IMCI chart booklet. For which age group is the 'sick child' section designed?
questions.e: The IMCI sick child chart covers children aged 2 months up to 5 years, while a separate sick young infant chart covers birth up to 2 months. Older children are managed with standard clinical guidance.

questions.s: A 2-year-old with ear pain had pus draining from the right ear for 4 days. There is no swelling behind the ear and she has no danger signs. How is this classified and treated under IMCI?
o: Chronic ear infection: dry the ear by wicking only
Mastoiditis: first dose of antibiotic and urgent referral to an ENT surgeon
Acute ear infection: oral amoxicillin for 5 days and dry the ear by wicking
questions.e: Ear discharge for less than 14 days, or ear pain, is an acute ear infection, treated with oral amoxicillin for 5 days, paracetamol for pain and drying by wicking. Discharge for 14 days or more is classified as chronic ear infection.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has fever and a tender swelling behind the left ear that pushes the pinna forward. Under IMCI, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Give oral amoxicillin and review in 5 days
Dry the ear and give ear drops
Give the first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and refer urgently
Apply a warm compress, give paracetamol and review the swelling in 2 days
questions.e: Tender swelling behind the ear is classified as mastoiditis, which needs a first dose of an appropriate antibiotic, paracetamol for pain and urgent referral, as it can lead to intracranial complications. Oral treatment at home is inadequate.

questions.s: Under IMCI, the classification boxes are coloured pink, yellow or green. What does a pink classification mean?
o: Specific treatment at the health facility and home care
questions.e: Pink classifications are severe and require urgent pre-referral treatment and referral, yellow ones require specific treatment at the facility (for example antibiotics) with home care, and green ones need only home management advice.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl has had watery diarrhoea for 2 days. She is lethargic and cannot drink, her eyes are sunken, and the skin pinch goes back very slowly. She has no other classification. In a BHU where IV fluids can be given, what is the IMCI classification?
questions.e: Two or more of lethargy or unconsciousness, sunken eyes, inability to drink and a very slow skin pinch indicate severe dehydration, treated with Plan C intravenous fluids if available, otherwise urgent referral with ORS on the way. Some dehydration features restlessness and eager drinking.

questions.s: A 3-month-old girl with Down syndrome has poor feeding, sweating during feeds and fast breathing. There is a murmur and the ECG shows a superior (left) axis. Which cardiac lesion is most likely?
questions.e: Atrioventricular septal defect is the cardiac lesion most characteristic of Down syndrome, and a superior QRS axis is typical. Every baby with Down syndrome should have an echocardiogram early because a large defect may cause heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.

questions.s: A healthy 5-year-old boy has a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, heard during a fever. It is louder lying down and quieter when he sits up. Heart sounds are normal, there is no thrill, and he is active and growing well. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A soft systolic murmur that varies with posture, in an asymptomatic child with normal heart sounds and no thrill, is an innocent murmur, often heard more easily during fever. Features such as a diastolic murmur, thrill, loud or pansystolic murmur or symptoms would need further assessment.

questions.s: A 7-week-old boy with a large VSD has tachypnoea, sweating during feeds, poor weight gain and a liver 4 cm below the costal margin. Which drug is the most appropriate initial treatment while awaiting surgical review?
questions.e: Heart failure from a large left-to-right shunt usually appears at 6-8 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; diuretics such as furosemide relieve congestion, with ACE inhibitors and calorie-dense feeds, until surgical closure. Prostaglandin E1 is for duct-dependent lesions.

questions.s: A newborn with transposition of the great arteries remains severely hypoxaemic (SpO2 55 %) despite a prostaglandin E1 infusion. Echocardiography shows a small, restrictive atrial communication. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase inspired oxygen to 100 % and observe
questions.e: In transposition, adequate mixing between the parallel circulations is essential; when the atrial septum is restrictive, balloon atrial septostomy enlarges the opening and improves oxygenation until the arterial switch operation. Extra oxygen does little when mixing is inadequate.

questions.s: A 12-year-old girl with short stature, a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples has hypertension in the right arm and weak femoral pulses. Which chromosomal condition is most likely?
questions.e: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature, a webbed neck, a broad chest and ovarian failure, and is associated with coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve. Down syndrome is mainly associated with AVSD, and Klinefelter syndrome affects males.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy with generalised oedema has a urine dipstick showing 4+ protein. Which spot urine result confirms nephrotic-range proteinuria?
o: Urine protein:creatinine ratio above 200 mg/mmol (2 mg/mg)
Urine protein:creatinine ratio above 20 mg/mmol (0.2 mg/mg)
questions.e: In children, nephrotic-range proteinuria is a urine protein:creatinine ratio above 200 mg/mmol (2 mg/mg) or 40 mg/m2/hour or more on a timed collection. A ratio of 20 mg/mmol marks the upper limit of normal, and an albumin:creatinine ratio of 3 mg/mmol detects microalbuminuria.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl with nephrotic syndrome still has 3+ proteinuria after 8 weeks of daily oral prednisolone given correctly. Renal function is normal. A renal biopsy is performed. Which histological finding is most likely?
questions.e: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children is most often due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which carries a risk of progression to kidney failure and needs calcineurin inhibitors or other agents. Minimal change disease is usually steroid sensitive.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy in relapse of nephrotic syndrome has abdominal pain, cold hands, a capillary refill time of 4 seconds and tachycardia, with a rising haematocrit, despite marked oedema. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Strict fluid restriction to 50 % of maintenance
questions.e: Despite oedema, children with nephrotic syndrome can be intravascularly depleted; abdominal pain, cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill and a rising haematocrit indicate hypovolaemia, which is treated with albumin infusion. Diuretics alone would worsen hypovolaemia and increase the risk of thrombosis.

questions.s: A 4-year-old with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is in remission. To reduce his risk of the most common serious bacterial infection associated with his condition, which measure is most important?
o: Avoidance of all live vaccines for life
questions.e: Children with nephrotic syndrome are prone to infections with encapsulated organisms, especially pneumococcal peritonitis and sepsis, so pneumococcal vaccination is recommended. Live vaccines are only deferred while on high-dose steroids, not avoided for life.

questions.s: A 6-week-old baby girl has generalised oedema, heavy proteinuria and very low serum albumin. She was born with a large placenta. Her parents are first cousins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome within the first 3 months of life is congenital nephrotic syndrome, often an autosomal recessive defect of the slit diaphragm protein nephrin (Finnish type), associated with a large placenta; it does not respond to steroids. Minimal change disease is unusual before 1 year.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has a seizure with fever. Which feature would make it a complex rather than a simple febrile seizure?
o: Jerking of the left arm only
A family history of febrile seizures
questions.e: A febrile seizure is complex if it is focal, lasts longer than 15 minutes or recurs within 24 hours or within the same illness. The height of the fever and a family history do not change the classification.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl is still having a generalised seizure after two doses of intravenous lorazepam given 5 minutes apart. Her airway is supported and she is receiving oxygen; glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate next drug?
o: A third dose of intravenous lorazepam
Oral carbamazepine through a nasogastric tube
questions.e: Convulsive status epilepticus not controlled by two doses of benzodiazepine is treated with a second-line agent such as intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or phenobarbital, with anaesthetic help if seizures persist. More than two benzodiazepine doses increase respiratory depression without much benefit.

questions.s: Between which ages do simple febrile seizures typically occur?
questions.e: Febrile seizures occur between about 6 months and 5 years of age with a temperature above 38 °C and no CNS infection. A seizure with fever in a young infant or an older child needs careful exclusion of meningitis and other causes.

questions.s: A 15-year-old girl has had morning jerks of her arms, causing her to drop her cup, and one generalised tonic-clonic seizure after a late night. EEG shows generalised polyspike-and-wave. Which drug is generally preferred to avoid teratogenic risk in her future?
questions.e: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy responds well to valproate, but valproate is highly teratogenic and is avoided in girls and women of childbearing potential, so levetiracetam or lamotrigine is preferred. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic seizures.

questions.s: An 11-year-old boy from a village where pigs are kept near the houses has a first focal seizure with jerking of the left hand. CT shows a single small ring-enhancing lesion with a central dot in the right parietal cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A single small ring-enhancing lesion with an eccentric dot (the scolex) presenting with focal seizures suggests neurocysticercosis due to Taenia solium; antiseizure drugs and, for viable cysts, albendazole with steroids are used. Tuberculomas are usually larger and lack a scolex.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy develops fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. He was at a wedding where a child had measles. Approximately how long after exposure do prodromal symptoms of measles usually start?
questions.e: The incubation period of measles is usually about 10-12 days to the start of the prodrome, with the rash appearing about 2-4 days later. This is why post-exposure vaccination within 72 hours can still help.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl with measles has had fever for 4 days and today develops a rash. How does a measles rash typically spread?
o: It starts behind the ears and on the face and spreads down to the trunk and limbs
It starts on the palms and soles and spreads centrally
It starts on the trunk as rose-pink macules after the fever has resolved and spares the face
It appears in crops of vesicles at different stages
questions.e: The maculopapular rash of measles begins behind the ears and along the hairline, spreads downwards over 2-3 days, and fades in the same order, leaving brownish staining and fine peeling. Crops of vesicles at different stages are typical of chickenpox.

questions.s: Six weeks after measles, a 2-year-old girl in a rural area has persistent diarrhoea and has lost weight; her MUAC is now 112 mm. Why is this child at high risk?
o: Measles virus persists in the gut and causes lifelong malabsorption
Measles causes immune suppression and increased nutritional demand, leading to malnutrition
The measles vaccine causes diarrhoea in malnourished children
Measles directly destroys the exocrine pancreas, causing permanent fat malabsorption and wasting
questions.e: Measles suppresses immunity for weeks to months and increases protein and vitamin A needs, so diarrhoea, secondary infections and malnutrition often follow, especially in poor settings. This child now has severe acute malnutrition and needs nutritional treatment.

questions.s: A malnourished 3-year-old boy with measles is admitted. His eyes are photophobic, and one cornea looks hazy with a small ulcer. Apart from eye care, which treatment is urgent?
questions.e: Measles in a vitamin A-deficient child can lead to corneal ulceration and keratomalacia, a major cause of childhood blindness; vitamin A must be given promptly, with a third dose later when eye signs are present, along with topical antibiotic. Steroid drops can worsen an infected ulcer.

questions.s: A child with measles is admitted to a paediatric ward in Lahore. Which infection control precaution is required?
o: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask only
Airborne precautions in a single room
questions.e: Measles spreads by the airborne route and is extremely contagious, so the child should be isolated in a single room (ideally negative pressure) with airborne precautions, and only immune staff should provide care. Surgical masks and droplet precautions are insufficient.

questions.s: An 8-year-old girl with thalassaemia major receives desferrioxamine by subcutaneous infusion. She develops fever, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Which infection is she particularly prone to while on this drug?
questions.e: Desferrioxamine acts as a siderophore that Yersinia can use to acquire iron, so patients on it are prone to Yersinia infection; the drug should be stopped and appropriate antibiotics given. The other organisms have no particular association with desferrioxamine.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy with poorly transfused beta-thalassaemia major has frontal bossing and a prominent maxilla. What is the classic finding on a lateral skull X-ray?
questions.e: Expansion of the marrow cavity from ineffective erythropoiesis produces the hair-on-end appearance of the skull vault and the typical facies; adequate transfusion prevents it. Punched-out lesions suggest myeloma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

questions.s: The parents of a 3-year-old girl with beta-thalassaemia major ask whether any treatment can cure her. Her 6-year-old brother is HLA-identical and does not have thalassaemia major. What is the established curative option?
o: Lifelong iron chelation combined with regular red cell transfusion
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation from her brother
questions.e: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation from an HLA-matched sibling is the established curative treatment, with the best results in young children with good chelation and no liver damage. Splenectomy, chelation and hydroxyurea do not cure the disease.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy with beta-thalassaemia major has no signs of puberty and is short. Serum testosterone, LH and FSH are all low. What is the most likely cause?
o: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from pituitary iron deposition
questions.e: Iron overload damages the anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with low LH, FSH and sex hormones; it is the commonest endocrine complication of thalassaemia. Primary testicular failure, as in Klinefelter syndrome, gives high LH and FSH.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy with thalassaemia major who has received many transfusions since infancy is found to have raised ALT on routine tests. Which infection should be tested for first?
questions.e: Transfusion-transmitted hepatitis C is a major cause of liver disease in multiply transfused children in Pakistan, together with hepatitis B and iron overload; regular screening is part of thalassaemia care. Hepatitis A and E spread by the faecal-oral route and do not cause chronic transfusion-related disease in this way.
